full_text_sections.conclusion: ConclusionsThe study evaluates physician knowledge, practice, and attitudes regarding viral exanthem diagnosis and mandatory reporting requirements in Florida. Respondents demonstrated moderate-to-high overall knowledge, with lower performance on clinical differentiation than on mandatory reporting. There was a strong statistical correlation between knowledge scores and physician confidence in diagnosis, underlining the importance of additional training for more accurate diagnosis and comprehensive management.Additionally, knowledge gaps were identified, particularly in the clinical differentiation of rubella. These knowledge gaps are present in all specialties, demonstrating a systemic nature rather than confinement to a single discipline.This topic is currently clinically relevant, as declining vaccination rates and increasing measles outbreaks carry important public health implications. Therefore, early diagnosis and reporting of VE are critical for outbreak prevention and control. Future studies are necessary on a larger scale, in different geographical areas, and among other physician specialties to evaluate differences, identify shared patterns, and address knowledge gaps in viral exanthem diagnosis.
full_text_sections.other: IntroductionViral exanthems (VEs) are rashes associated with systemic viral infections such as measles, rubella, and roseola [1]. They are often characterized by a diffuse eruption of macules and papules that can be erythematous in nature [2]. VEs can be differentiated based on distinct patterns; however, definitive diagnosis cannot always be made solely on the rash’s appearance and symptoms. It is important for clinicians to incorporate a comprehensive patient history, including travel from endemic areas, vaccination records, prodromal symptoms, and potential exposure history, to aid diagnostic accuracy. While these infections are typically self-limiting, atypical or severe patterns can present in immunocompromised patients, children, and pregnant women [3]. Despite the availability of safe and tested vaccine options, VE, such as measles, was the cause of 142,300 deaths worldwide in 2018, with the majority of cases found among young children and immunocompromised adults, driven by increased travel from endemic areas, limited vaccine availability in under-resourced areas, and declining vaccination rates in regions where they were previously eliminated, indicating the continuing public health importance of these viruses [4, 5].The measles virus is a paramyxovirus belonging to the genus Morbillivirus [6]. The measles virus is a highly contagious viral infection transmitted via respiratory or aerosolized droplets. It uses host receptors including CD150 (SLAMF1) to infect susceptible immune cells of the respiratory tract, which then transport the virus to the lymphoid cells, further causing systemic disease and contributing to its high virulence and contagiousness [7]. After the virus gains entry, there is an incubation period of up to 3 weeks, which is followed by the prodromal phase of a high fever, often greater than 39 degrees Celsius [6]. Other early symptoms are cough, malaise, and the pathognomonic Koplik spots, which are small, white spots located on the buccal mucosa. The rash in measles begins on the face before spreading to the rest of the body. Due to overlapping symptoms with the common cold and other illnesses that have symptoms of a fever and rash, measles can be misdiagnosed [8]. Currently, the preferred method of diagnosing measles is nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT). Serologic IgM can be used to make the diagnosis, but clinical caution should be exercised as patients within 72 hours of developing a rash can return false-negative serology up to 20% of the time [9]. Rubella virus is a non-vector-borne member of the family Togaviridae and the sole member of the genus Rubivirus [10]. Rubella virus contains RNA, which is surrounded by a capsid and a lipoprotein envelope. Rubella is asymptomatic in 25% to 50% of young children with an incubation period of 2 to 3 weeks. Early symptoms are a mild fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy, and sore throat that precede a pinpoint erythematous maculopapular rash. The classic rubella rash starts on the face and neck and proceeds to spread to the trunk and lower extremities over the course of 3 days [11]. Complications such as congenital rubella syndrome (CRS), which affects newborns when a pregnant woman is exposed to the rubella virus, manifest in the triad of cataracts, congenital defects, and deafness. Since clinical manifestations can range from mild to atypical presentations, clinical diagnosis is made not only on the symptoms, but also serological testing for rubella-specific IgM and/or IgG antibodies remains the gold standard of diagnosis [9].Roseola infantum, also known as exanthema subitum or sixth disease, is predominantly caused by infection with human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), or, less commonly, by human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7) [12]. About ninety percent of cases occur in children younger than two years. Its clinical course begins with a high fever of up to 40 degrees Celsius, lasting 3 to 5 days, followed classically by a maculopapular erythematous rash originating on the trunk as the fever resolves. A complication of roseola infantum is acute febrile seizures due to its ability to cross the blood-brain barrier. Roseola infantum is a clinical diagnosis without any need for serology. Unlike measles and rubella, roseola has no vaccine available, but it continues to affect young children predominantly, accounting for 10 to 45% of febrile illnesses in infants, warranting the need for proper public health measures to avoid spreading the virus [12].Although cases of VE, primarily measles, mumps, and rubella, have drastically decreased in the United States due to high vaccination rates, outbreaks and cases continue to occur in areas with high travel from endemic or under-resourced areas, including the State of Florida. These cases pose a public health threat in regions where proper public health measures, including vaccine coverage, continue to fall. While vaccine-preventable VE rates have plummeted following implementation of mandatory school vaccines in 1997 for middle school entry, Florida was the first state in the United States to move to end all mandates for vaccine requirements for children and adults on September 3rd, 2025, with planned removal of select vaccine mandates in January 2026 [13, 14, 15]. As of August 5th, 2025, there have been 1356 confirmed measles cases in 41 jurisdictions, with 32 outbreaks reported in 2025 compared to 16 outbreaks in 2024 [16]. Of the 1356 cases in 2025, 92% were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccine history, the majority under age 20 years old, with most of the cases being in Texas (800+) [16]. In 2024-2025, Florida had 30 confirmed cases of measles [17]. People are most protected through herd immunity when over 95% of the community is vaccinated; however, Measles, Mumps, and Rubella (MMR) vaccination coverage among kindergarteners in the USA has decreased to 92.7% in 2023-2024 from 95.2% during 2019-2020 [16]. In the United States, vaccines are readily available, but drivers of vaccine hesitancy include misinformation about side effects, reduced vaccination rates during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, health disparities among underserved groups in rural and urban settings, and a lack of awareness regarding the severity of infection, leading to potential public health risks [18]. The current and recent outbreaks of VE stress the importance of proper public health strategies to prevent future outbreaks, including continuing education of healthcare professionals, especially in primary care, pediatrics, and family medicine, where patients are more likely to present with complications of VE.Previous studies have examined healthcare professionals’ knowledge of vaccine-preventable diseases and measles. However, few studies have looked at both viral exanthem diagnosis and mandatory reporting requirements. This gap helped support the need for the present study. Thus, in light of current circumstances, it is increasingly critical for physicians and healthcare workers to remain vigilant in recognizing vaccine-preventable infectious diseases to aid in public health measures and avoid further outbreaks of these diseases. The purpose of this study is to determine the current knowledge, attitudes, and practices among practicing physicians regarding viral exanthem diagnosis and their mandatory reporting requirements in various metropolitan areas of Florida, USA. The primary objective was to assess Florida physicians’ knowledge of the clinical differentiation and mandatory reporting requirements of measles, rubella, and roseola. Secondary objectives were to compare knowledge across medical specialties and examine associations between self-reported confidence and knowledge scores. We hypothesize that our data will reveal differences between physicians of different specialties or of different levels of exposure to these viruses.

papers.title_original: Physician Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding Viral Exanthem Diagnosis and Mandatory Reporting Requirements in Major Metropolitan Regions of Florida, USA

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess physician knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding viral exanthem (VE) diagnosis and mandatory reporting requirements in Florida, highlighting the need to understand gaps in clinical awareness of these conditions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 162 physicians in Florida, with 146 providing complete responses for inferential analyses. Participants were identified from the Florida Department of Health practitioner database based on license status, county, and specialty.
analysis.methods: Statistical analyses included analysis of variance (ANOVA), multivariate ANOVA (MANOVA), Tukey post hoc testing, and linear regression. The relationships between vignette-style diagnosis knowledge questions and confidence attitude questions were analyzed through linear regression.
analysis.main_results: Pediatricians demonstrated the highest overall knowledge scores (82.66%), followed by internal medicine (76.39%) and family medicine physicians (73.26%). Of 162 responses, geographic practice settings included urban 83 (51.2%), suburban 83 (51.2%), and rural 18 (11.1%).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that overall knowledge differences among specialties were significant, with pediatricians scoring higher than family medicine physicians. However, no significant differences were found when examining vignette-based knowledge questions separately.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings inform the need for targeted training programs for physicians, particularly in family medicine, to improve their knowledge and confidence in diagnosing and reporting viral exanthems such as measles.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the non-random respondent sample, uneven specialty representation, and potential nonresponse bias. The evidence is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated physician knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding viral exanthem (VE) diagnosis and mandatory reporting in Florida. A survey of 162 physicians revealed significant differences in overall knowledge scores among specialties, with pediatricians scoring highest. However, no significant differences were observed when vignette-based knowledge questions were analyzed separately. The study highlights the need for additional training in VE diagnosis and management, particularly for family medicine physicians. Limitations include a non-random sample and potential nonresponse bias, which affect the strength of the evidence. The findings suggest that targeted educational interventions could improve clinical awareness and reporting practices for measles and other viral exanthems.

analysis.event: A measles outbreak with cases near 1,400 was reported by the American Hospital Association. The event is confirmed based on the outbreak data.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak has resulted in nearly 1,400 cases, indicating a significant public health impact. The risk level is explicitly stated as high due to the potential for further spread and the vulnerability of the population.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The American Hospital Association is actively reporting on the outbreak, but no specific details on investigation, testing, or containment measures are provided. The status remains under review and requires further analysis.

analysis.brief_en: The American Hospital Association reported a measles outbreak in Pennsylvania with nearly 1,400 cases as of October 30, 2026. This outbreak is confirmed and highlights a significant public health impact. The high risk level suggests potential for further spread, especially among vulnerable populations. While the association is monitoring the situation, specific details on investigation, testing, or containment measures are not provided. The outbreak underscores the importance of vaccination and public health preparedness. The report does not mention any confirmed cases of related viruses such as canine distemper or rubella, nor does it include information on hard-excluded entities. The source status is full, indicating the original article body was extracted, and the content is based on the association's official statements.

news.title_zh: 宾夕法尼亚州接近 1,400 例病例 麻疹 暴发 - 美国医院协会
news.source_body_en: The American Hospital Association reported a measles outbreak in Pennsylvania with nearly 1,400 cases as of October 30, 2026. This outbreak is confirmed and highlights a significant public health impact. The high risk level suggests potential for further spread, especially among vulnerable populations. While the association is monitoring the situation, specific details on investigation, testing, or containment measures are not provided. The outbreak underscores the importance of vaccination and public health preparedness. The report does not mention any confirmed cases of related viruses such as canine distemper or rubella, nor does it include information on hard-excluded entities. The source status is full, indicating the original article body was extracted, and the content is based on the association's official statements.

Clinical trials Employees Professionals Media inquiries Financial assistance Contact us News & stories Help me find Doctors Specialties Locations Schedule My Health Connection Log in UCHealth Today All Innovative care Healthy living Stories News Live Colorado Español UCHealth Today > Thousands may have been exposed to measles at Denver International Airport as U.S. cases continue to surge Why is measles so dangerous? Does it spread more easily than the viruses that cause flu, COVID-19, Ebola and polio? And who should get vaccinated to prevent measles? By: Katie Kerwin McCrimmon Yesterday An employee who later tested positive for measles traveled through Denver International Airport, one of the world’s busiest, multiple times in early October, potentially exposing thousands of people to the highly infectious illness. Photo courtesy of Denver International Airport. The number of measles cases across the U.S. this year has surged to nearly double the number of cases in 2025. And a person who was infected with the highly contagious illness traveled three times in early October through Denver International Airport — one of the busiest airports in the world — potentially exposing thousands of people to measles, according to health officials with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. The person is an adult who lives in Jefferson County, Colorado, and health officials did not reveal the person’s vaccination status. The person arrived on a flight at Gate C-50 on Oct. 3 at 12:25 a.m., then rode the busy airport train to the B Concourse and left the airport on an employee shuttle. The person then traveled through Denver International Airport twice the next day. On Oct. 4, the infectious person rode an employee shuttle from a parking lot to Denver International Airport, then departed on a flight from Gate B-48 at 10:57 a.m. The person returned to Denver International Airport at 11:25 p.m. on the night of Oct. 4, arriving at Gate A-18. The employee once again rode the train to Concourse B and took an employee shuttle. Health officials urge anyone who may have been exposed to this person and becomes sick to contact their medical provider immediately. “If you were at (these locations) you may have been exposed,” Colorado health officials wrote in a news release. It’s particularly critical for unvaccinated people to be aware of exposures since measles spreads so easily. Health officials urged anyone who is sick and who might be infected with measles to call their medical provider before showing up at a clinic. Measles cases continue to climb in Colorado and across the U.S. As of October 22, federal health officials at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have confirmed 4,588 measles cases across the country in 2026, double the compared 2,289 in all of 2025. About 10% of people who got sick across the U.S. had to be hospitalized. And Pennsylvania health officials have linked 1260 cases and five deaths with an ongoing measles outbreak there. In Colorado, health officials have confirmed 26 measles cases so far in 2026. That compares with 36 cases in all of 2025. Once a measles outbreak starts, it’s very difficult to stop it. That’s because measles is so contagious. It spreads more easily than diseases including COVID-19, flu, polio and Ebola. Along with being extremely infectious, measles is also very dangerous. “Measles can be deadly in children, and many people end up hospitalized. They’re very sick. It can be quite frightening,” said Dr. Michelle Barron. Barron is one of Colorado’s top infectious disease experts and is UCHealth’s senior medical director for infection control and prevention. She also is a professor of medicine and infectious diseases at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine. These new spikes in measles cases in Colorado and across the U.S. disappoint health officials because the U.S. eradicated measles in 2000. The disease is preventable through a safe and effective vaccine. Why does measles spread so quickly, and where are measles cases highest this year? It’s very difficult to fight measles outbreaks because the disease is so contagious among unvaccinated people. The highest numbers of measles cases through mid-October in the U.S. have occurred in these 12 states, according to CDC and state health department data: Pennsylvania: 1,260 measles cases. South Carolina: 670 measles cases. Utah: 535 measles cases. Wisconsin: 256 measles cases. Texas: 192 measles cases. Virginia: 178 measles cases. Kentucky: 167 measles cases. Ohio: 160 measles cases. Florida: 148 measles cases. New York: 122 measles cases. Arizona: 110 measles cases. California: 55 measles cases. Some of the outbreaks have spread in schools. “When you’re in enclosed spaces for long periods of time, which schools generally are, it’s going to spread,” Barron said. “Everybody’s in classrooms, hallways, bathrooms. Anybody who is breathing the air where an infected person has been could get exposed.” For people who have not been vaccinated, the likelihood of getting measles after exposure is essentially certain, Barron said. That’s because the measles virus has adapted to survive for long periods in the air. “When someone coughs, spits, or sneezes, the virus becomes airborne. Let’s say you are in line with me at the grocery store, and I have measles, and I am coughing or sneezing. The virus can hang out in the air for up to two hours after that, and you can then breathe in the virus,” she said. “If you are not protected by the vaccine, the measles virus then can infect you. CDC researchers estimate that nine of 10 people who lack protection against measles will develop measles infection if exposed to a close contact,’’ Barron said. Her advice is very simple: “Get your vaccine. And if you’re concerned, talk to your provider. They have your best interests at heart.” I thought we had nearly eradicated measles. Why is this dangerous illness coming back? Like other vaccine-preventable diseases, illnesses like measles are on the rise because many parents are not vaccinating their children. Dr. Heather Holmstrom, a family medicine expert at UCHealth Family Medicine Clinic in Boulder, urges all of her patients to get vaccinated. Dr. Heather Holmstrom “We eradicated these diseases, and now they’re coming back,” said Holmstrom, who is also an associate professor of family medicine at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. There are areas in Colorado with poor vaccination rates, like Boulder. And at the same time, these areas have diverse, relatively wealthy populations, with many people traveling around the world. Measles cases are on the rise around the globe. So, increased travel means it’s more likely that Coloradans can bring dangerous diseases home from abroad. Holmstrom spends considerable time educating parents about the importance of vaccines. She also encounters young adults who weren’t vaccinated as children. “I encourage all young adults whose parents didn’t vaccinate them to get vaccinated,” Holmstrom said. Get the facts – Trusted sources on vaccinations Colorado Children’s Immunization Coalition U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment She often has to dispel common myths that have long since been disproven. There is no evidence that vaccines cause autism. Holmstrom and her colleagues have to repeat that message repeatedly and constantly encourage parents to get their babies and children fully vaccinated. “Routine childhood immunizations are really important for protecting every individual child as well as our community,” she said. “People ask me if I’ve vaccinated my own children, and I’m always really open with them. My own children have gotten every routine vaccine ever available.” And she tells them, “Yours should too.” Many doctors have not seen measles since it was eradicated in the U.S. in 2000. But with new outbreaks, more doctors are caring for patients with measles, which appears as a rash, in this case on a person’s back. Photo by Getty Images. Why are measles outbreaks so concerning: a snapshot of the numbers Barron said measles is dangerous because it causes severe medical challenges for those who get it, especially unvaccinated people. Here are some medical complications that can strike people who get measles: At least one in five unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles will need to be hospitalized. As many as one in every 20 children who become infected with measles will also get pneumonia, which is the most common cause of death from measles in young children. About 1 in 1,000 children who get measles will develop encephalitis, or swelling of the brain. Encephalitis can lead to very frightening convulsions and can leave a child Deaf or with an intellectual disability. As many as three of every 1,000 children who become infected with measles will die from respiratory and neurologic complications. Measles may cause pregnant women who have not been vaccinated to give birth prematurely or to give birth to a low birth-weight baby. Among people who have gotten sick with measles this year, 94% have been unvaccinated, nearly identical to 2025, when 93% of those with confirmed measles cases also had not received their measles vaccines, according to experts at the CDC. Learn how people with measles can also deal with immunity amnesia. Barron said measles enters the body in a way that also destroys cells that protect our immune systems. The infection essentially destroys what Barron calls our “special forces” that detect and fight infections. That’s why it’s common for people who get measles to also get secondary infections after getting measles. Their bodies don’t have the defenses to fight additional infections. What are the signs and symptoms of measles? Most people get a fever, cough, runny nose or red eyes at first. A rash that looks like red bumps appears on the chest and can appear on the arms and back. Characteristic spots can develop in the mouth. These spots often look like white spots in the back of the throat. Symptoms typically appear 7 to 14 days after exposure. But it may take up to 21 days for an infected person to get sick. A person with measles is contagious for four days before and four days after the rash appears. Signs and symptoms of measles include: Fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. The appearance of a rash at the hairline, spreading downward over the body, usually begins 2-4 days after other symptoms. What should you do if you think you might have been exposed to measles? If you think you might have been exposed to measles, it’s vital to stay home so you can avoid spreading the illness. Barron and state health officials are asking parents and individuals who think they might have measles to call ahead before visiting a doctor’s office, urgent care clinic or hospital ER. And be sure to tell health care providers that you might have been exposed to measles. “We really want to minimize the number of other people who are exposed. Even if it turns out that you’re sick with something different, we want to make sure we’re taking precautions. If you think you have measles, you should call ahead. And we would ask that you wear a mask because that helps minimize exposure to others,” Barron said. “Be sure to tell people up front that you’re concerned that you might have measles. We’ll put you in a different room and will expedite the process of having you see a provider.” Symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash that usually starts on the face and spreads. What about people who are fully vaccinated for measles? Are they safe to go to school or activities? Barron said people who are fully vaccinated should be fine attending school and visiting public places. “If they’re immunized, they’re safe,” Barron said. “There’s no reason for them (anyone who is fully vaccinated) not to continue with their activities,” she said. Learn why Vitamin A and cod liver oil don’t prevent measles + what it’s like to be sick with this dangerous illness. What if you haven’t been vaccinated for measles? Are you likely to get it? Yes. People who haven’t had the MMR vaccine (which stands for measles, mumps and rubella) are highly likely to get measles if they are exposed to someone with a confirmed case. If an unvaccinated person who is exposed to measles gets the MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure to someone with measles, they might be able to prevent a full case of measles. How can you check your MMR vaccination status? Vaccination is highly effective against measles, and people who have previously been vaccinated with the MMR vaccine do not need to receive the vaccine again after exposure to measles. Coloradans can check their/their child’s vaccine status through an online database. Should patients have one or two MMR shots? People who were born prior to 1957 are considered immune. If you were born between 1957 and 1989, you may have only had one shot. You should ask your doctor to either perform a blood test that determines whether your body is protected from the measles virus and whether you need another shot — a booster shot — or simply opt to have an MMR shot without the blood test. If you were born in 1989 or after, you probably have had two shots, but it’s a good idea to verify this. What if a patient was born after 1989 and has had only one shot? See your doctor. Your doctor can perform a blood test to check to see if you need to be protected from the measles virus and whether you need another shot. Or patients can simply opt to have an MMR shot without the blood test. There’s no danger in receiving an additional vaccination. What if patients don’t know if they’ve had the MMR vaccine? Your doctor can order a blood test to check to see if you need to be protected from measles. How long does it take for the vaccination to go into effect so you’re protected from measles? After a person gets the MMR vaccine, it takes about one week for the vaccine to become fully effective. After receiving the first shot, how long do you need to wait to get the second shot? Patients need to wait at least 28 days to get a second shot. Where can I get MMR vaccines? The MMR vaccine is safe and effective at preventing measles (as well as mumps and rubella). Two doses of MMR are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles infection. CDC experts recommend that children receive a first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months of age and a second dose at 4 to 6 years of age. People who receive MMR vaccination according to the U.S. vaccination schedule are usually considered protected for life against measles. The vaccine is widely available in Colorado for free or low cost. Call your medical provider or speak to your doctor during a routine wellness exam for you or your children. The federal Vaccines for Children program provides vaccines at no cost for children from birth through 18 years who are uninsured, underinsured, on Medicaid or Medicaid eligible, and/or Alaskan Native/American Indian. Here’s another snapshot of recent data about measles from the CDC and state health authorities: This year is proving to be tough for the spread of measles, with hundreds of cases already reported across the U.S. South Carolina is having the worst measles outbreak this year, but multiple other states also are seeing high numbers of measles cases. Measles hits children especially hard. Among people with confirmed measles cases in 2025, 26% were under age 5, and an additional 44% were ages 5 to 19. Of those with confirmed measles in 2025, 11% were hospitalized. Measles was officially eradicated in the U.S. in 2000, but after false information about measles vaccines took hold, vaccination rates dropped, and cases have climbed since then. It’s likely that the U.S. now will lose its status as a place where measles has been eradicated. The highest number of cases in recent years prior to 2025 was in 2019, when U.S. health officials reported 1,274 confirmed measles cases nationwide. The U.S. has already surpassed the 2019 high-water mark just two months into 2026. The number of measles cases in the U.S. in 2025 was the highest since 1991, when health officials logged 9,643 cases. That’s when doctors began giving patients two doses of the measles vaccine. Who can I call in Colorado if I’m worried about measles? If you are worried that you may have been exposed to measles and you are experiencing symptoms, immediately notify your health care provider by telephone. Explain that you may have had a possible measles exposure and describe your symptoms. Call a medical provider before physically showing up to minimize the chance of exposure to other people. If you do not have a health care provider, call an urgent care center or emergency department. For additional information about measles, call the free helpline CO-HELP at 303-389-1687 (toll-free: 1-877-462-2911). “Anyone who is experiencing symptoms of measles should stay home unless they need medical treatment,” said Dr. Rachel Herlihy, Colorado State Epidemiologist. “People with signs and symptoms of measles should also not go to child care facilities, school, work, or other public places to avoid exposing others to this very serious and highly contagious disease.” Infectious diseases Measles vaccines Virus prevention You may also like: Flu season hits Colorado early. Clinical trials Employees Professionals Media inquiries Financial assistance Contact us News & stories Help me find Doctors Specialties Locations Schedule My Health Connection Log in UCHealth Today All Innovative care Healthy living Stories News Live Colorado Español UCHealth Today > Thousands may have been exposed to measles at Denver International Airport as U.S. cases continue to surge Why is measles so dangerous? Does it spread more easily than the viruses that cause flu, COVID-19, Ebola and polio? And who should get vaccinated to prevent measles? By: Katie Kerwin McCrimmon Yesterday An employee who later tested positive for measles traveled through Denver International Airport, one of the world’s busiest, multiple times in early October, potentially exposing thousands of people to the highly infectious illness. Photo courtesy of Denver International Airport. The number of measles cases across the U.S. this year has surged to nearly double the number of cases in 2025. And a person who was infected with the highly contagious illness traveled three times in early October through Denver International Airport — one of the busiest airports in the world — potentially exposing thousands of people to measles, according to health officials with the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. The person is an adult who lives in Jefferson County, Colorado, and health officials did not reveal the person’s vaccination status. The person arrived on a flight at Gate C-50 on Oct. 3 at 12:25 a.m., then rode the busy airport train to the B Concourse and left the airport on an employee shuttle. The person then traveled through Denver International Airport twice the next day. On Oct. 4, the infectious person rode an employee shuttle from a parking lot to Denver International Airport, then departed on a flight from Gate B-48 at 10:57 a.m. The person returned to Denver International Airport at 11:25 p.m. on the night of Oct. 4, arriving at Gate A-18. The employee once again rode the train to Concourse B and took an employee shuttle. Health officials urge anyone who may have been exposed to this person and becomes sick to contact their medical provider immediately. “If you were at (these locations) you may have been exposed,” Colorado health officials wrote in a news release. It’s particularly critical for unvaccinated people to be aware of exposures since measles spreads so easily. Health officials urged anyone who is sick and who might be infected with measles to call their medical provider before showing up at a clinic. Measles cases continue to climb in Colorado and across the U.S. As of October 22, federal health officials at the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) have confirmed 4,588 measles cases across the country in 2026, double the compared 2,289 in all of 2025. About 10% of people who got sick across the U.S. had to be hospitalized. And Pennsylvania health officials have linked 1260 cases and five deaths with an ongoing measles outbreak there. In Colorado, health officials have confirmed 26 measles cases so far in 2026. That compares with 36 cases in all of 2025. Once a measles outbreak starts, it’s very difficult to stop it. That’s because measles is so contagious. It spreads more easily than diseases including COVID-19, flu, polio and Ebola. Along with being extremely infectious, measles is also very dangerous. “Measles can be deadly in children, and many people end up hospitalized. They’re very sick. It can be quite frightening,” said Dr. Michelle Barron. Barron is one of Colorado’s top infectious disease experts and is UCHealth’s senior medical director for infection control and prevention. She also is a professor of medicine and infectious diseases at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine. These new spikes in measles cases in Colorado and across the U.S. disappoint health officials because the U.S. eradicated measles in 2000. The disease is preventable through a safe and effective vaccine. Why does measles spread so quickly, and where are measles cases highest this year? It’s very difficult to fight measles outbreaks because the disease is so contagious among unvaccinated people. The highest numbers of measles cases through mid-October in the U.S. have occurred in these 12 states, according to CDC and state health department data: Pennsylvania: 1,260 measles cases. South Carolina: 670 measles cases. Utah: 535 measles cases. Wisconsin: 256 measles cases. Texas: 192 measles cases. Virginia: 178 measles cases. Kentucky: 167 measles cases. Ohio: 160 measles cases. Florida: 148 measles cases. New York: 122 measles cases. Arizona: 110 measles cases. California: 55 measles cases. Some of the outbreaks have spread in schools. “When you’re in enclosed spaces for long periods of time, which schools generally are, it’s going to spread,” Barron said. “Everybody’s in classrooms, hallways, bathrooms. Anybody who is breathing the air where an infected person has been could get exposed.” For people who have not been vaccinated, the likelihood of getting measles after exposure is essentially certain, Barron said. That’s because the measles virus has adapted to survive for long periods in the air. “When someone coughs, spits, or sneezes, the virus becomes airborne. Let’s say you are in line with me at the grocery store, and I have measles, and I am coughing or sneezing. The virus can hang out in the air for up to two hours after that, and you can then breathe in the virus,” she said. “If you are not protected by the vaccine, the measles virus then can infect you. CDC researchers estimate that nine of 10 people who lack protection against measles will develop measles infection if exposed to a close contact,’’ Barron said. Her advice is very simple: “Get your vaccine. And if you’re concerned, talk to your provider. They have your best interests at heart.” I thought we had nearly eradicated measles. Why is this dangerous illness coming back? Like other vaccine-preventable diseases, illnesses like measles are on the rise because many parents are not vaccinating their children. Dr. Heather Holmstrom, a family medicine expert at UCHealth Family Medicine Clinic in Boulder, urges all of her patients to get vaccinated. Dr. Heather Holmstrom “We eradicated these diseases, and now they’re coming back,” said Holmstrom, who is also an associate professor of family medicine at the University of Colorado School of Medicine. There are areas in Colorado with poor vaccination rates, like Boulder. And at the same time, these areas have diverse, relatively wealthy populations, with many people traveling around the world. Measles cases are on the rise around the globe. So, increased travel means it’s more likely that Coloradans can bring dangerous diseases home from abroad. Holmstrom spends considerable time educating parents about the importance of vaccines. She also encounters young adults who weren’t vaccinated as children. “I encourage all young adults whose parents didn’t vaccinate them to get vaccinated,” Holmstrom said. Get the facts – Trusted sources on vaccinations Colorado Children’s Immunization Coalition U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment She often has to dispel common myths that have long since been disproven. There is no evidence that vaccines cause autism. Holmstrom and her colleagues have to repeat that message repeatedly and constantly encourage parents to get their babies and children fully vaccinated. “Routine childhood immunizations are really important for protecting every individual child as well as our community,” she said. “People ask me if I’ve vaccinated my own children, and I’m always really open with them. My own children have gotten every routine vaccine ever available.” And she tells them, “Yours should too.” Many doctors have not seen measles since it was eradicated in the U.S. in 2000. But with new outbreaks, more doctors are caring for patients with measles, which appears as a rash, in this case on a person’s back. Photo by Getty Images. Why are measles outbreaks so concerning: a snapshot of the numbers Barron said measles is dangerous because it causes severe medical challenges for those who get it, especially unvaccinated people. Here are some medical complications that can strike people who get measles: At least one in five unvaccinated people in the U.S. who get measles will need to be hospitalized. As many as one in every 20 children who become infected with measles will also get pneumonia, which is the most common cause of death from measles in young children. About 1 in 1,000 children who get measles will develop encephalitis, or swelling of the brain. Encephalitis can lead to very frightening convulsions and can leave a child Deaf or with an intellectual disability. As many as three of every 1,000 children who become infected with measles will die from respiratory and neurologic complications. Measles may cause pregnant women who have not been vaccinated to give birth prematurely or to give birth to a low birth-weight baby. Among people who have gotten sick with measles this year, 94% have been unvaccinated, nearly identical to 2025, when 93% of those with confirmed measles cases also had not received their measles vaccines, according to experts at the CDC. Learn how people with measles can also deal with immunity amnesia. Barron said measles enters the body in a way that also destroys cells that protect our immune systems. The infection essentially destroys what Barron calls our “special forces” that detect and fight infections. That’s why it’s common for people who get measles to also get secondary infections after getting measles. Their bodies don’t have the defenses to fight additional infections. What are the signs and symptoms of measles? Most people get a fever, cough, runny nose or red eyes at first. A rash that looks like red bumps appears on the chest and can appear on the arms and back. Characteristic spots can develop in the mouth. These spots often look like white spots in the back of the throat. Symptoms typically appear 7 to 14 days after exposure. But it may take up to 21 days for an infected person to get sick. A person with measles is contagious for four days before and four days after the rash appears. Signs and symptoms of measles include: Fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. The appearance of a rash at the hairline, spreading downward over the body, usually begins 2-4 days after other symptoms. What should you do if you think you might have been exposed to measles? If you think you might have been exposed to measles, it’s vital to stay home so you can avoid spreading the illness. Barron and state health officials are asking parents and individuals who think they might have measles to call ahead before visiting a doctor’s office, urgent care clinic or hospital ER. And be sure to tell health care providers that you might have been exposed to measles. “We really want to minimize the number of other people who are exposed. Even if it turns out that you’re sick with something different, we want to make sure we’re taking precautions. If you think you have measles, you should call ahead. And we would ask that you wear a mask because that helps minimize exposure to others,” Barron said. “Be sure to tell people up front that you’re concerned that you might have measles. We’ll put you in a different room and will expedite the process of having you see a provider.” Symptoms of measles include fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes, and a characteristic rash that usually starts on the face and spreads. What about people who are fully vaccinated for measles? Are they safe to go to school or activities? Barron said people who are fully vaccinated should be fine attending school and visiting public places. “If they’re immunized, they’re safe,” Barron said. “There’s no reason for them (anyone who is fully vaccinated) not to continue with their activities,” she said. Learn why Vitamin A and cod liver oil don’t prevent measles + what it’s like to be sick with this dangerous illness. What if you haven’t been vaccinated for measles? Are you likely to get it? Yes. People who haven’t had the MMR vaccine (which stands for measles, mumps and rubella) are highly likely to get measles if they are exposed to someone with a confirmed case. If an unvaccinated person who is exposed to measles gets the MMR vaccine within 72 hours of exposure to someone with measles, they might be able to prevent a full case of measles. How can you check your MMR vaccination status? Vaccination is highly effective against measles, and people who have previously been vaccinated with the MMR vaccine do not need to receive the vaccine again after exposure to measles. Coloradans can check their/their child’s vaccine status through an online database. Should patients have one or two MMR shots? People who were born prior to 1957 are considered immune. If you were born between 1957 and 1989, you may have only had one shot. You should ask your doctor to either perform a blood test that determines whether your body is protected from the measles virus and whether you need another shot — a booster shot — or simply opt to have an MMR shot without the blood test. If you were born in 1989 or after, you probably have had two shots, but it’s a good idea to verify this. What if a patient was born after 1989 and has had only one shot? See your doctor. Your doctor can perform a blood test to check to see if you need to be protected from the measles virus and whether you need another shot. Or patients can simply opt to have an MMR shot without the blood test. There’s no danger in receiving an additional vaccination. What if patients don’t know if they’ve had the MMR vaccine? Your doctor can order a blood test to check to see if you need to be protected from measles. How long does it take for the vaccination to go into effect so you’re protected from measles? After a person gets the MMR vaccine, it takes about one week for the vaccine to become fully effective. After receiving the first shot, how long do you need to wait to get the second shot? Patients need to wait at least 28 days to get a second shot. Where can I get MMR vaccines? The MMR vaccine is safe and effective at preventing measles (as well as mumps and rubella). Two doses of MMR are approximately 97% effective at preventing measles infection. CDC experts recommend that children receive a first dose of the MMR vaccine at 12 to 15 months of age and a second dose at 4 to 6 years of age. People who receive MMR vaccination according to the U.S. vaccination schedule are usually considered protected for life against measles. The vaccine is widely available in Colorado for free or low cost. Call your medical provider or speak to your doctor during a routine wellness exam for you or your children. The federal Vaccines for Children program provides vaccines at no cost for children from birth through 18 years who are uninsured, underinsured, on Medicaid or Medicaid eligible, and/or Alaskan Native/American Indian. Here’s another snapshot of recent data about measles from the CDC and state health authorities: This year is proving to be tough for the spread of measles, with hundreds of cases already reported across the U.S. South Carolina is having the worst measles outbreak this year, but multiple other states also are seeing high numbers of measles cases. Measles hits children especially hard. Among people with confirmed measles cases in 2025, 26% were under age 5, and an additional 44% were ages 5 to 19. Of those with confirmed measles in 2025, 11% were hospitalized. Measles was officially eradicated in the U.S. in 2000, but after false information about measles vaccines took hold, vaccination rates dropped, and cases have climbed since then. It’s likely that the U.S. now will lose its status as a place where measles has been eradicated. The highest number of cases in recent years prior to 2025 was in 2019, when U.S. health officials reported 1,274 confirmed measles cases nationwide. The U.S. has already surpassed the 2019 high-water mark just two months into 2026. The number of measles cases in the U.S. in 2025 was the highest since 1991, when health officials logged 9,643 cases. That’s when doctors began giving patients two doses of the measles vaccine. Who can I call in Colorado if I’m worried about measles? If you are worried that you may have been exposed to measles and you are experiencing symptoms, immediately notify your health care provider by telephone. Explain that you may have had a possible measles exposure and describe your symptoms. Call a medical provider before physically showing up to minimize the chance of exposure to other people. If you do not have a health care provider, call an urgent care center or emergency department. For additional information about measles, call the free helpline CO-HELP at 303-389-1687 (toll-free: 1-877-462-2911). “Anyone who is experiencing symptoms of measles should stay home unless they need medical treatment,” said Dr. Rachel Herlihy, Colorado State Epidemiologist. “People with signs and symptoms of measles should also not go to child care facilities, school, work, or other public places to avoid exposing others to this very serious and highly contagious disease.” Infectious diseases Measles vaccines Virus prevention You may also like: Flu season hits Colorado early. news.content: Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape News Canada How Canada Can Prevent the Next Measles Outbreak Carolyn Crist October 29, 2026 10 Add to Email Alerts Jump to Key Points The nationwide measles outbreak — which resulted in more than 6400 cases across 10 provinces and territories in 2 years — has officially ended, according to the Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC). The agency made its announcement after more than 2 months had passed since the last associated case was reported. Infectious diseases experts in Canada are cautiously optimistic but recommend vigilance for future outbreaks. “It’s helpful and a step in the right direction that this outbreak is now declared finished, but this is not the finish line. This is the starting gate,” Isaac Bogoch, MD, professor of medicine at the University of Toronto and infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital, told Medscape News Canada. “Measles represents the canary in the coal mine. It shows the chinks in the armor of public health systems,” he said. “You have to think about other vaccine-preventable diseases — such as influenza, polio, and tuberculosis — and I’m not sure if we’ve really taken the necessary steps to prevent subsequent outbreaks.” Measles Outbreak Response Measles was first eliminated in Canada in 1998. During the nearly 30 year-period when measles was considered eliminated (1998-2024), the country reported an average of 91 cases annually, with 0-752 each year. Following sustained transmission of the same virus strain for more than 1 year, PHAC announced in November 2025 that the country’s measles elimination status had been lost. SUGGESTED FOR YOU Isaac Bogoch, MD “We never should have been in a position where a high-income country with a sound healthcare and public health system should lose our measles elimination status, but here we are,” said Bogoch. “The drivers are similar here and worldwide — we’ve been chipping away at public health initiatives through a lack of funding and a lack of trust.” The multijurisdictional outbreak began in New Brunswick with a patient who was exposed to measles outside Canada. Additional cases with symptom onset after October 24, 2024, were considered part of the outbreak if the measles virus sequence matched that of the first case or if epidemiologic evidence (such as direct contact with an outbreak-related case) supported a connection. As of October 26, 1126 measles cases have been reported so far this year, according to Canada’s measles and rubella weekly monitoring report. Two new cases unrelated to the multijurisdictional outbreak were reported in Quebec during October 11-17. Seven measles cases are being monitored in British Columbia, Ontario, and Quebec. During the past 2 years, more than 90% of cases occurred among people who were unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. “In the big picture of what we can do as healthcare professionals, the fundamental root of the issue is vaccination. We originally achieved measles elimination by having almost everyone vaccinated across Canada,” Matthew Muller, MD, PhD, medical director of infection prevention and control and an infectious diseases physician at St. Michael’s Hospital and Unity Health Toronto, told Medscape News Canada. “If we can achieve herd immunity with 95% of people being vaccinated, there’s no need for anyone to get measles, including vulnerable people who can’t be vaccinated,” he said. “I want healthcare workers to remember that measles isn’t just a rash and a fever — it can be a severe disease that leads to severe complications, and I don’t want to go back to seeing those develop.” Two doses of a measles-containing vaccine can provide strong protection against infection. Canadians — including healthcare professionals — should check with their provider or local public health unit to verify their measles vaccination status, PHAC said. Matthew Muller, MD, PhD “With vaccination, if the percentage falls below herd immunity, it’s like a forest getting too dry, and then a spark can ignite a wildfire,” Muller said. “If we have big areas in Canada where people aren’t vaccinated, then one case can trigger the fire that leads to a widespread outbreak.” Muller also serves as chair in the Ontario Provincial Infectious Diseases Advisory Committee on Infection Prevention and Control and has helped with guideline and policy development around infection prevention in Ontario hospitals. He and his colleagues have talked about the importance of vaccination — and of having conversations with patients about their vaccination status. “It’s important to have open and frank conversations, not shying away or making assumptions about why someone may not be vaccinated,” he said. “Listen to understand their concerns and then help debunk myths and be a resource for them.” Future Outbreak Preparation Along with vaccination conversations, healthcare providers in hospitals and community settings can remain prepared by looking for measles symptoms and handling suspected cases appropriately. “While it’s great that this current outbreak is under control, there will continue to be introduction of measles into the population, especially with our closest geographic neighbor [the United States] having an ongoing outbreak in various states. We need to keep our index of suspicion high for measles when presented with compatible symptoms,” Susy Hota, MD, medical director for infection prevention and control and division head of infectious diseases at University Health Network in Toronto, told Medscape News Canada. Clinics and ambulatory settings, in particular, may feel more vulnerable and less prepared when handling unannounced cases that walk in the door, she noted. As part of an infection control policy, clinics can implement protocols that encourage patients and staff to know their vaccination status, provide time for staff to receive vaccinations, and design clinic intake to protect vulnerable groups from infection. Susy Hota, MD For instance, when confirming patient appointments, staff scripts should ask about broad respiratory symptoms, as well as measles-specific signs, such as a new rash. If new symptoms are disclosed at sign-in, staff can isolate suspected cases and put systems in place to care for pregnant patients, those with weakened immune systems, and vulnerable patients who may experience severe symptoms, such as infants or older adults. Updating these protocols now can help when an unexpected case occurs in the future, Hota said. “While reviewing a previous case, we found that measles hadn’t been recognized as part of the initial differential review, and the patient traveled from that clinic area to the lab for blood collection, which was adjacent to the preadmission area and led to massive exposure that was difficult to track,” she said. “When you plan ahead, include measles as a possible diagnosis, and follow protocols, you can isolate the patient, wear the appropriate protective gear, obtain bloodwork in a safe way, and mitigate the risks of spread.” Bogoch, Muller, and Hota reported having no relevant financial relationships. Carolyn Crist is a health and medical journalist who reports on the latest studies for Medscape, MDedge, and WebMD. analysis.time: The nationwide measles outbreak ended in 2026, with the last associated case reported more than 2 months prior to the announcement. The article was published on October 29, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred across 10 provinces and territories in Canada, affecting a population that included unvaccinated individuals and those with unknown vaccination status, particularly among vulnerable groups such as infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals.
analysis.event: The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) declared the nationwide measles outbreak officially ended. This was based on the absence of new cases for over 2 months and the conclusion of the outbreak's transmission period. The article reports this as a confirmed event.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in more than 6400 cases over 2 years, with 90% of cases occurring among unvaccinated or unknown vaccination status individuals. PHAC noted that the outbreak highlighted weaknesses in public health systems and the risk of future outbreaks due to low vaccination rates and potential reintroduction from neighboring countries.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: PHAC has concluded the outbreak and is now focusing on preventing future outbreaks through vaccination efforts. Experts recommend maintaining high vigilance, updating protocols, and ensuring healthcare workers and patients are aware of their vaccination status. The response is ongoing and involves public health initiatives and policy development.

analysis.brief_en: The article discusses the conclusion of a nationwide measles outbreak in Canada, which ended in 2026 after more than 2 months without new cases. The outbreak, which affected 10 provinces and territories, resulted in over 6400 cases over 2 years, with 90% of cases linked to unvaccinated or unknown vaccination status individuals. Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) declared the outbreak over, emphasizing the need for vigilance against future outbreaks. Experts highlight the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent the resurgence of measles, which can lead to severe complications. They recommend healthcare professionals and patients to verify vaccination status and update protocols to protect vulnerable groups. The article also notes the ongoing risk of measles introduction from neighboring countries like the United States, which has its own outbreak. The response includes public health initiatives, policy development, and improved infection control measures in clinics and hospitals.

analysis_en.time: The nationwide measles outbreak ended in 2026, with the last associated case reported more than 2 months prior to the announcement. The article was published on October 29, 2026.
analysis_en.location_and_population: The outbreak occurred across 10 provinces and territories in Canada, affecting a population that included unvaccinated individuals and those with unknown vaccination status, particularly among vulnerable groups such as infants, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals.
analysis_en.event: The Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) declared the nationwide measles outbreak officially ended. This was based on the absence of new cases for over 2 months and the conclusion of the outbreak's transmission period. The article reports this as a confirmed event.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in more than 6400 cases over 2 years, with 90% of cases occurring among unvaccinated or unknown vaccination status individuals. PHAC noted that the outbreak highlighted weaknesses in public health systems and the risk of future outbreaks due to low vaccination rates and potential reintroduction from neighboring countries.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: PHAC has concluded the outbreak and is now focusing on preventing future outbreaks through vaccination efforts. Experts recommend maintaining high vigilance, updating protocols, and ensuring healthcare workers and patients are aware of their vaccination status. The response is ongoing and involves public health initiatives and policy development.

news.title_zh: 加拿大如何预防下一个 麻疹 暴发 - Medscape
news.source_body_en: The article discusses the conclusion of a nationwide measles outbreak in Canada, which ended in 2026 after more than 2 months without new cases. The outbreak, which affected 10 provinces and territories, resulted in over 6400 cases over 2 years, with 90% of cases linked to unvaccinated or unknown vaccination status individuals. Public Health Agency of Canada (PHAC) declared the outbreak over, emphasizing the need for vigilance against future outbreaks. Experts highlight the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent the resurgence of measles, which can lead to severe complications. They recommend healthcare professionals and patients to verify vaccination status and update protocols to protect vulnerable groups. The article also notes the ongoing risk of measles introduction from neighboring countries like the United States, which has its own outbreak. The response includes public health initiatives, policy development, and improved infection control measures in clinics and hospitals.

news.content_zh: 截至 2026 年 10 月 30 日,美国已报告超过 4,800 例 麻疹 病例,宾夕法尼亚州和威斯康星州分别记录了 88 例和 82 例新感染病例。病例激增引发了人们对 麻疹 准确度和疾病传播的担忧,因为一项研究发现 7% 的 麻疹 病例被误诊。CIDRAP 指出,由于 疫苗接种 的阻力越来越大,卫生专业人员正在努力管理 暴发。目前情况仍在调查中,呼吁加强公共卫生准备并信任 疫苗接种 的努力。该报告强调了解决 疫苗 犹豫不决和确保有效遏制策略方面的更广泛挑战。

news.content_title: Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada’s loss of measles elimination status: descriptive cohort study
news.content: Sarah E Wilson , public health physician 1 2 3 4 , Gillian H Lim , epidemiologist 1 , Mehdi Aloosh , medical officer of health 5 6 , Adelle Chang On , associate medical officer of health 7 , Cara-Lee Coghill , public health nurse 8 , Tara Harris , program manager 1 , Maan Hasso , microbiologist 1 9 , Miriam Klassen , medical officer of health 10 , Christine Navarro , public health physician 1 2 3 , Eleanor Paget , nurse consultant 1 , Kaitlin Patterson , epidemiologist 11 , Marina I Salvadori , paediatric infectious disease physician 11 12 , Ninh Tran , medical officer of health 8 , John Tuinema , associate medical officer of health 13 14 , Daniel Warshafsky , associate chief medical officer of health 2 15 , Joanne Hiebert , microbiologist 16 Author affiliations 1 Public Health Ontario, Toronto, Ontario, M5G 1M1, Canada 2 Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 3 Centre for Vaccine Preventable Diseases, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 4 ICES, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 5 Windsor-Essex County Health Unit, Windsor, Ontario, Canada 6 Department of Health Research Methods, Evidence and Impact, McMaster University, Hamilton, Ontario, Canada 7 Region of Waterloo Public Health, Waterloo, Ontario, Canada 8 Southwestern Public Health, St Thomas, Ontario, Canada 9 Department of Laboratory Medicine and Pathobiology, Faculty of Medicine, University of Toronto, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 10 Huron Perth Public Health, Stratford, Ontario, Canada 11 Centre for Immunization Surveillance and Programs, Public Health Agency of Canada, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada 12 Department of Pediatrics, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada 13 Algoma Public Health, Sault Ste Marie, Ontario, Canada 14 Northern Ontario School of Medicine, Sudbury, Ontario, Canada 15 Office of the Chief Medical Officer of Health, Ontario Ministry of Health, Toronto, Ontario, Canada 16 Measles, Mumps and Rubella Section, National Microbiology Laboratory Branch, Public Health Agency of Canada, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada Correspondence to: S Wilson ( sarah.wilson@oahpp.ca ) Abstract Objective To describe the epidemiological characteristics, public health response, and evidence of international spread of a large measles outbreak that contributed to the loss of Canada’s measles elimination status. Design Descriptive analysis of the cohort of measles outbreak cases reported to Ontario’s public health surveillance system during the outbreak period: epidemiological week of 28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025. Participants Individuals meeting the outbreak case definition for confirmed or probable measles infection during the outbreak period. Exposure Exposure to measles virus associated with the Ontario outbreak and related transmission chains. Main outcome measures Demographic characteristics, vaccination status, admission to hospital, complications, pregnancy associated outcomes, mortality, and evidence of international spread based on measles virus genotyping and sequencing. Cases were identified using an outbreak-specific case definition incorporating epidemiological, clinical, laboratory, and viral sequencing criteria. Phylogenetic analysis of measles virus sequences was used to assess evidence of onwards spread to other countries. Results The outbreak consisted of 2377 cases (2064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks and contributed to the loss of Canada’s measles elimination status. Most cases (2146/2377, 90.3%) occurred among members of historically under-vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2377 cases, approximately three quarters of cases (n=1736, 73.0%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2121 (89.2%) were unvaccinated, and 97 (4.1%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 (7%) admissions to hospital, 13 (<1%) admissions to intensive care unit, 51 (2.1%) infections during pregnancy, 10 (<1%) congenital measles infections, one (<1%) case of encephalitis, and one (<1%) infant death. Sequencing identified a novel N450 distinct sequence identifier that was subsequently detected in countries including the United States of America, Mexico, and the Netherlands. The outbreak strain was designated a World Health Organization named strain (MVs/Ontario.CAN/47.24). Conclusions These findings highlight the risk of measles re-establishment in countries that have attained elimination and underscore the importance of culturally appropriate community engagement to build trust in immunisation and prevent future outbreaks. This outbreak shows the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of long standing immunity gaps within interconnected communities across the Americas and the population-level protection that limited broader community transmission. Introduction Measles is a highly infectious respiratory virus. Its high transmissibility reflects short and long range transmission of infectious respiratory particles through the air and a period of communicability extending from four days before until four days after rash onset. 1 Consequently, susceptible contacts are frequently exposed to the virus before cases are recognised and public health control measures, including case isolation and post-exposure prophylaxis, can be effectively implemented. Measles can cause severe complications, admission to hospital, and death, particularly among infants, pregnant individuals, and people who are immunocompromised. 1 Beyond its direct health effects, measles is associated with substantial social and economic burdens on individuals and families. In a patient-based survey, acute measles infection was associated with a mean illness duration of 13.8 days, 9.6 days away from school or work, and substantial reductions in health related quality of life. 2 Despite the availability of a safe and highly effective vaccine, measles outbreaks have re-emerged in several countries that had previously achieved elimination. 3 Canada attained measles elimination status in 1998 after the introduction of a second dose of measles-containing vaccine and a national catch-up programme for school-aged children. 4 5 High uptake of the two dose schedule led to a marked decline in measles incidence. In the province of Ontario, more than 5000 cases were reported in 1991, 6 compared with 101 cases reported between 2013 and 2023. 7 In November 2025, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) determined that Canada lost its measles elimination status due to ongoing domestic transmission associated with a multijurisdictional measles outbreak. 8 The outbreak began in October 2024, after exposure to measles at a wedding in New Brunswick, Canada, followed by secondary cases among attendees in the provinces of New Brunswick and Ontario. 7 Ontario is home to several diverse ethno-religious and cultural groups with vaccine coverage that has historically been low due to a combination of structural barriers, historical experience with health systems, and community specific perspectives on vaccination. These groups, which include some Mennonite, Amish, and Netherlands Reformed communities, have close social networks spanning Canada, the United States of America (USA), Mexico, and other countries that create opportunities for cross-border transmission. 9 10 11 We describe the epidemiological and genomic characteristics of the Ontario measles outbreak, which formed part of a broader multijurisdictional outbreak involving other Canadian provinces, 12 the US, Mexico and several other countries across the Americas. 13 14 We also summarise the public health response and some of the unique challenges posed by this outbreak, and their implications for re-establishing measles elimination, which are relevant for other countries at risk of losing elimination status. To support case finding activities, an outbreak-specific case definition was established, 17 allowing inclusion of clinically compatible cases with relevant epidemiological linkages. On 10 June 2025, the outbreak case definition was updated to incorporate sequencing information, classifying laboratory-confirmed cases as outbreak-related if viral sequences matched defined distinct sequence IDs (DSId), 18 even in the absence of direct epidemiological linkage; this change was also applied retrospectively. Diagnostic testing was conducted at Public Health Ontario regional laboratories with RT-PCR testing introduced at one non-Public Health Ontario laboratory on 16 June 2025. All specimens positive for measles underwent secondary RT-PCR testing to differentiate wild-type virus from vaccine strain and all wild-type virus detections were referred to the National Microbiology Laboratory for genotyping and sequencing (further details outlined in the eMethods in the supplementary appendix). 19 20 21 To increase the uptake of laboratory testing, patient self-collection of specimens was accepted, facilitated by local public health agencies, and evaluated as part of quality assurance activities. Vaccination status was determined using doses of measles-containing vaccine administered at least 14 days before symptom onset. Local public health agency staff also determined if suspect cases were members of historically under-vaccinated communities. For cases in pregnant women, additional information was collected, including pregnancy and infant outcomes. Confirmed congenital measles cases were identified using a case definition provided by the Public Health Agency of Canada. 12 For the one report of death, a case conference approach, with clinicians involved in direct patient care, determined the extent to which measles contributed to the cause of death. Although Panorama captures vaccines administered by local public health staff during outbreak responses, most vaccines are administered in primary care and are added retrospectively based on records collected by local public health agencies under the Immunization of School Pupils Act. The completeness of these data is known to have been affected by a pause in record-collection processes during the covid-19 pandemic, particularly for younger children, and by incomplete capture of vaccinations among children attending private religious schools. 22 23 Recent trends in coverage of measles-containing vaccine at the provincial and local public health agency levels were obtained from Public Health Ontario’s immunisation data tool, 24 which uses Panorama as its data source and is subject to the same limitations. We calculated and mapped these measures by forward sortation area using the 2021 Canadian Census. Phylogenetic analysis of N450 sequences was performed to describe the Ontario outbreak strain and assess the extent to which it has been implicated in measles activity outside of Canada (further details outlined in the eMethods in the supplementary appendix). All five local public health agencies are located in rural and semi-rural communities in the province and four of the five share geographical boundaries in southwestern Ontario. Multiple cases were associated with exposures in community and healthcare settings, resulting in well documented chains of transmission. The outbreak involved 2377 cases, with 2064 confirmed and 313 probable, and was linked to historically under-vaccinated communities. Most cases (90.3%) occurred among these communities, with limited spillover into the general population. news.source_body_en: A large measles outbreak in Ontario, Canada, from October 2024 to October 2025 led to the loss of Canada's measles elimination status. The outbreak involved 2377 cases, with 2064 confirmed and 313 probable, and was linked to historically under-vaccinated communities. Most cases (90.3%) occurred among these communities, with limited spillover into the general population. The outbreak strain, designated as MVs/Ontario.CAN/47.24, was found to have spread internationally to the United States, Mexico, and the Netherlands. The outbreak was associated with 166 hospital admissions, 13 ICU admissions, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis, and one infant death. Public health measures, including case isolation and post-exposure prophylaxis, were implemented. The outbreak highlights the risk of measles re-establishment in countries with elimination status and underscores the importance of community engagement to improve vaccination rates and prevent future outbreaks.

news.content: News Health Ontario recorded 2,377 measles cases — News-Medical UA.NEWS 29 October 2026 05:36 In Ontario, Canada, a measles outbreak lasted 49 weeks — from October 28, 2024, to October 6, 2025 — and included 2,377 cases. It contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025, News-Medical reports , citing a study published in The BMJ. Most cases were among unvaccinated people Researchers analyzed data from Ontario's surveillance system. Of the 2,377 cases, 2,064 were confirmed and 313 were probable. About 90% of cases occurred among members of communities with historically low vaccination rates that have close social ties in Canada, the United States, Mexico, and other countries. Spread beyond these communities was limited. Of all patients, 73% were aged 19 years or younger. A total of 2,121 patients, or 89% of the total, were unvaccinated; for another 97 people, or 4%, vaccination status was unknown. Canada acquired measles-free status in 1998 after introducing a two-dose vaccination schedule and a national catch-up vaccination program for schoolchildren. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Hospitalizations and strain spread A total of 166 hospitalizations were linked to this outbreak, including 13 admissions to intensive care units. There were also 51 cases of infection during pregnancy, 10 cases of congenital measles, one case of encephalitis, and the death of one infant. Laboratory studies identified a distinct measles virus strain that was later recorded in other parts of Canada, as well as in the United States, Mexico, and the Netherlands. Researchers cautioned that the actual number of cases and complications may be higher than recorded in surveillance data. In their view, preventing new outbreaks requires strengthening immunization systems, increasing vaccination coverage, and culturally adapted engagement with communities to build trust in vaccination.
