news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Stranded Cruise World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Watch CBS News HealthWatch As measles outbreaks grow in the U.S., maps and charts show a record number of cases in 2026 By Grace Manthey Grace Manthey Senior Visual Data Journalist, Data Team Coordinator Grace Manthey is the senior visual data journalist and data team coordinator for CBS News and Stations. She is an Emmy-winning journalist and visual storyteller with a passion for telling stories that matter. Read Full Bio Grace Manthey Updated on: October 29, 2026 / 2:04 PM EDT / CBS News Add CBS News on Google So far in 2026, the U.S. has recorded the most measles cases in more than three decades as outbreaks spread in multiple states, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. By mid-July, the number had already surpassed all of 2025, which had been the worst year in recent history with more than 2,200 confirmed cases. By October, the number of cases topped 4,500. Ongoing outbreaks have put the U.S. at risk of losing its official measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. In August, health officials in Pennsylvania reported the state's first two deaths connected to measles in 35 years, both in Lancaster County. Both of the individuals were not vaccinated against the virus, state health officials said. Several more deaths associated with measles were later reported as the state's outbreak surged. Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. In some cases, it can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death. But it can be prevented by vaccination, which medical research has proven to be safe and highly effective. The CBS News data team has tracked confirmed measles cases nationwide as new data is released by state health departments and the CDC. Out of the 2,289 confirmed cases last year, more than 750 were connected to an outbreak in West Texas that led to the deaths of two children. Prior to 2025, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. in recent years was 1,274 in 2019, driven by outbreaks in New York, California and Washington state. Most years, the total was much lower. Health experts point to lower vaccination rates as the main reason for increases in preventable infectious diseases like measles. The vast majority of cases have been in people who were unvaccinated, and outbreaks have spread in communities with lower vaccination rates. CDC data shows about 92.4% of kindergartners in the U.S. got their measles-mumps-rubella shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down slightly from 92.5% the previous year. The figure has declined from 95.2% during the 2019-2020 school year — a critical threshold to keep people safe. Only 10 states hit the 95% threshold last year. "When more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated, most people are protected through community immunity (herd immunity)," the CDC states. "I think that parents, for most kids, especially for the measles vaccines, the DTP, all the standard childhood vaccines, it's very important that parents vaccinate their kids," Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health, said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan." Research has found no evidence of increased rates of autism among those who are vaccinated compared to those who are not. Vaccines also undergo intensive safety testing. Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu US measles cases top 4,800 as the disease surges in multiple states Jim Wappes Measles CDC / Cynthia S. Goldsmith, William Bellini Share Copied to clipboard It used to be that 200-plus US measles cases would reflect the total for the year or even for two years, but the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) today confirmed 264 new cases in just the past seven days, raising the country’s total to 4,852 cases, by far the highest yearly total in 35 years. The new data mark the 12th straight week of triple-digit increases nationwide. Rising cases in multiple states have contributed to the escalation, but Pennsylvania continues to be the nation’s hot spot, logging 88 new cases this week, followed closely by Wisconsin. The United States will very likely lose its measles elimination status—which it gained in 2000—in the coming month. Even an analysis published in May, when the country had only around 1,800 cases, said as much. The CDC has logged 43 measles outbreaks across the country so far this year, compared with 48 for all of last year, which saw 2,289 cases by year’s end. An outbreak involves three or more people. All but 18 infections this year have been locally acquired, with the rest involving international travelers. Of the confirmed cases, 17% have been in children under the age of 5 years, and 41% have been in kids and teens ages 5 to 19. Eleven percent of cases overall have required hospitalization, a number that has been slowly climbing and now matches the 2025 rate. Hospitalization rates are highest in preschoolers (16%), with a 14% rate in adults 20 and older. Though the CDC continues to acknowledge just three measles deaths this year, Pennsylvania has reported five, with a sixth death in that state under investigation. The vast majority of confirmed cases (96%) have been in people who are unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status. Illnesses surge in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Indiana In its ongoing outbreak, this week Pennsylvania confirmed 88 new cases and 1,426 total cases, by far the largest state outbreak the nation has seen since the early 1990s. Lancaster County continues to be the epicenter, with 493 cases now. Mifflin is second with 205 cases, followed by Chester (93) and Jefferson (88). As opposed to the national trend, 67% of reported cases in Pennsylvania have involved adults. The state’s outbreak doesn’t appear to be slowing, despite a statement from Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. two weeks ago that he will bring it “to a quick close.” An Associated Press story today, however, said more of the state’s residents are open to vaccination, including those in hard-hit Amish communities. Wisconsin saw another large jump this week, with 82 new cases and 392 total. Of those cases, 336, or 86% of the total, have been confirmed in Grant, Iowa, Lafayette, and Vernon counties in southwestern Wisconsin. State and county officials in that area “are working to identify and notify people who may have been exposed to the measles virus,” the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said. Chippewa County has 33 infections. Neighboring Minnesota has reached its highest measles total in 36 years, the Minnesota Department of Health reported yesterday. The state now has 80 cases, with 38 new cases in the past week. “The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is well-tested, highly effective, and provides long-lasting protection,” said Minnesota Commissioner of Health Brooke Cunningham, MD, PhD. “We strongly advise anyone who is recommended to receive the MMR vaccine and has not been vaccinated to contact their healthcare provider and get vaccinated now.” The measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is well-tested, highly effective, and provides long-lasting protection. The disease is also surging in Indiana. With 47 newly confirmed cases, the state is just shy of 100 for the year. Today the Indiana Department of Public Health listed 97 known measles infections, with the most in LaGrange (22 cases), Adams (17), and Wayne (16) counties. Ohio confirmed 30 more infections this week, and 296 total. New York state has eight new cases, lifting its count to 170. Finally, Iowa, which before August 16 had only one case for 2026, has now recorded 42, according to Iowa Health and Human Services. Last year Iowa had nine measles cases. Cases in Kentucky have now reached 201, the state health department reported today, with four new cases this past week. Last year the state recorded only 11 measles infections. The hardest-hit counties are Christian (65 cases), Laurel (56), and Trigg (31). news.title: Measles Update: October 30, 2026
news.excerpt: The latest CDC numbers show a 5.8% increase in measles cases from week-to-week, bringing the 2026 US total to more than double the amount seen in all of 2025 with 2 months left in the year.

Pylori Norovirus Healthcare Associated Infections (HAI) Prevention Antibiotics Immunizations Vaccines Respiratory Infections Community-Acquired Pneumonia Measles Influenza Sexually Transmitted Diseases HIV / AIDS HPV HSV PrEP Skin & Soft Tissue Diseases MRSA Zoonotic & Vector-Borne Diseases Lyme Disease ZIKA Choose Topic Spotlight - Vaccines in America| Antibiotics Deconstructed| Bench to Bedside With SIDP| Antimicrobial Stewardship| Hepatitis Advertisement News|Articles|October 30, 2026 Measles Update: October 30, 2026 Author(s)Matt Hoffman The latest CDC numbers show a 5.8% increase in measles cases from week-to-week, bringing the 2026 US total to more than double the amount seen in all of 2025 with 2 months left in the year. Advertisement Today, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported there were 4,852* cases of measles in the US as of October 29, 2026. Week-over-week, this is an additional 264 cases and a 5.8% increase. Last week, the federal agency reported there were 4,588* confirmed cases.1-2 CDC said there were 4,834 measles cases were reported by 47 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming. A total of 18 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States. 1 The federal agency reports there have been 43 new outbreaks** reported in 2026, and 96% of confirmed cases (4,666 of 4,852) are outbreak-associated (3,282 from outbreaks starting in 2026 and 1,384 from outbreaks started in 2025).1 2026 Case Totals Already Double All of 2025 For the full year of 2025, the CDC reported 2,289 confirmed* measles cases across 45 jurisdictions, along with 48 outbreaks. This year's total of 4,852 cases is more than twice the 2025 figure. By comparison, 16 outbreaks were reported during 2024, and 69% of cases (198 of 285) were outbreak-associated.1 Measles Testing Measles PCR Testing Climbs as Positivity Rises in National Lab Data Age, Vaccination, and Hospitalization Data According to the CDC's case table, 17% of cases (766) occurred in children younger than 5 years, 42% (1914) in those aged 5 to 19 years, and 41% (1881) in adults aged 20 years or older. Overall, 96% of cases were in unvaccinated people or people with unknown vaccination status, 2% had received 1 MMR dose, and 2% had received 2 doses. Hospitalization was reported for 10% of cases (479 of 4,588), including 16% of children younger than 5 years. The CDC reports 3 measles deaths in 2026, a number it says is subject to change.1 *It is important to note the CDC says on its website the federal agency is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions. However, the data on this page only include confirmed cases jurisdictions notified the CDC about. Therefore, there could be higher numbers in the US overall. **CDC reports the cumulative number of measles outbreaks (defined as 3 or more related cases) that have occurred this year in the US; states have the most up-to-date information about cases and outbreaks in their jurisdictions. news.content: IDWeek By Gary S. Marshall, MD Fact checked by Jennifer Mesce Purpose-built for physicians Learn more Read more November 16, 2025 5 min read What clinicians need to know as measles cases hit 33-year high November 19, 2024 4 min read Q&A: ‘We have to be worried’ about decline in measles vaccination September 18, 2025 2 min read CDC advisors table vote to delay hepatitis B vaccination in newborns October 28, 2026 2 min read Carolina schools with high vaccination rates fared better vs. measles Road back to measles elimination starts with us October 29, 2026 4 min read By Gary S. I had not seen measles until 1989, when I was a fellow at The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. It was the beginning of the first major resurgence of measles in the United States during the vaccine era. Philadelphia went on to experience a 2-year outbreak that claimed the lives of nine children. (If you want to understand the human side of that story, read Paul Offit’s 2015 book Bad Faith .) Between 1989 and 1991, there were 55,622 measles cases and 123 associated deaths across the country. We are in the midst of the worst outbreak since then , with the number of confirmed cases this year approaching 5,000. The average number of measles-related deaths per year in the U.S. from 2000 to 2020 was less than 1; this year, there have already been 5 deaths in Pennsylvania alone . In November, an international commission will determine if the U.S. still meets criteria for measles elimination, a status it has held for over 2 decades. An analysis performed earlier this year suggests the answer is likely to be no. A main driver of measles transmission in 1991 were pockets of susceptible inner-city preschoolers with suboptimal access to healthcare. Today, a main driver is people who could have been — but were intentionally not — protected by vaccination, the cumulative effect of post-COVID vaccine skepticism, widespread misinformation and disinformation, and a federal posture that is best described as anti-scientific. If you trained in the early 2000s or thereafter, you have probably never seen the disease. That’s because measles cases plummeted after the adoption of a two-dose MMR schedule in 1989 and the implementation of school mandates. It follows, then, that you probably have not seen the consequences of measles, which, death aside, include pneumonia, encephalitis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). That’s the one that really gets me. Your seemingly healthy 6-year-old develops personality change, declining school performance, myoclonus, ataxia, dysarthria, dementia and eventually coma, the result of a defective measles virus that has persisted in their central nervous system since they had an uneventful case of measles at a young age. SSPE is estimated to occur in about 1 in 600 children who are infected under 12 months. We do not know how many American children will experience this slow dying of the neurological light as a result of the current measles outbreak. In the Philippines, they are just now seeing the leading edge of a wave of SSPE cases following the measles outbreak in 2018 and 2019. A study by Lee and colleagues presented at IDWeek called attention to the importance of school as a place where outbreaks amass energy. It stands to reason that vaccination requirements (if they actually result in vaccination) and the rapid identification and exclusion of cases can squelch that energy. Recent analyses suggest that the epidemic threshold is crossed in schools years before outbreaks are apparent at the county level; this means that incipient outbreaks may be invisible to our current surveillance methods. A study by Creech and colleagues , also presented at IDWeek, begs the question of whether the first dose of MMR should be given earlier. There are trade-offs here. If we continue to wait until 12 months and the prevalence of disease increases, there will be more infant cases with their associated severity. If we vaccinate at 6 months, residual maternal antibodies could prevent “take” in a substantial proportion of infants, leaving them susceptible later on. Even in the absence of antibody interference, early vaccination could result in less perfect and shorter-lived humoral immunity. A dose at 6 months could be added to the existing 12-month and 4- to 6-year schedule, but what should be the threshold for pushing that button? In thinking about this, the cited abstracts intersect because the secondary attack rate in schools underscores that “all measles transmission is local,” and if we wait until traditional surveillance demonstrates that an outbreak is occurring, it may be too late for some infants. This conundrum would not exist if we continued along the road to sustained elimination, which could only happen if immunization rates remain high. We cannot get there by offering parents P -values and confidence intervals; instead, it will take heartfelt, impassioned appeals to the love they have for their children and a steadfast confidence on the part of their providers that vaccination is the right thing. The theory of quantum mechanics agrees with physical measurements to within 1 part per trillion. In other words, the most successful scientific theory in the history of the world might be wrong, but chances are, it’s right. This lends some perspective to the concerns that many parents have about the science behind vaccine safety. Studies show that MMR does not cause autism, to within the margin of error afforded by studies of millions of person-years of observation. Just like proofs of quantum mechanics, there will always be some margin of error. The question comes down to balancing the incredibly small probability of error with the very real threat to health and well-being that measles represents. For more information: Gary S. Marshall, MD, is a professor of pediatrics and chief of the division of pediatric infectious diseases at Norton Children’s and the University of Louisville School of Medicine. He is the author of Healio’s Clinical Guidance module on measles and The Vaccine Handbook . He can be reached at pids@idsociety.org . An analysis performed earlier this year suggests the answer is likely to be no. A main driver of measles transmission in 1991 were pockets of susceptible inner-city preschoolers with suboptimal access to healthcare. Today, a main driver is people who could have been — but were intentionally not — protected by vaccination, the cumulative effect of post-COVID vaccine skepticism, widespread misinformation and disinformation, and a federal posture that is best described as anti-scientific. If you trained in the early 2000s or thereafter, you have probably never seen the disease. That’s because measles cases plummeted after the adoption of a two-dose MMR schedule in 1989 and the implementation of school mandates. It follows, then, that you probably have not seen the consequences of measles, which, death aside, include pneumonia, encephalitis and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE). That’s the one that really gets me. Your seemingly healthy 6-year-old develops personality change, declining school performance, myoclonus, ataxia, dysarthria, dementia and eventually coma, the result of a defective measles virus that has persisted in their central nervous system since they had an uneventful case of measles at a young age. SSPE is estimated to occur in about 1 in 600 children who are infected under 12 months. We do not know how many American children will experience this slow dying of the neurological light as a result of the current measles outbreak. In the Philippines, they are just now seeing the leading edge of a wave of SSPE cases following the measles outbreak in 2018 and 2019. A study by Lee and colleagues presented at IDWeek called attention to the importance of school as a place where outbreaks amass energy. It stands to reason that vaccination requirements (if they actually result in vaccination) and the rapid identification and exclusion of cases can squelch that energy. Recent analyses suggest that the epidemic threshold is crossed in schools years before outbreaks are apparent at the county level; this means that incipient outbreaks may be invisible to our current surveillance methods. A study by Creech and colleagues , also presented at IDWeek, begs the question of whether the first dose of MMR should be given earlier. There are trade-offs here. If we continue to wait until 12 months and the prevalence of disease increases, there will be more infant cases with their associated severity. If we vaccinate at 6 months, residual maternal antibodies could prevent “take” in a substantial proportion of infants, leaving them susceptible later on. Even in the absence of antibody interference, early vaccination could result in less perfect and shorter-lived humoral immunity. A dose at 6 months could be added to the existing 12-month and 4- to 6-year schedule, but what should be the threshold for pushing that button? In thinking about this, the cited abstracts intersect because the secondary attack rate in schools underscores that “all measles transmission is local,” and if we wait until traditional surveillance demonstrates that an outbreak is occurring, it may be too late for some infants. This conundrum would not exist if we continued along the road to sustained elimination, which could only happen if immunization rates remain high. We cannot get there by offering parents P -values and confidence intervals; instead, it will take heartfelt, impassioned appeals to the love they have for their children and a steadfast confidence on the part of their providers that vaccination is the right thing. The theory of quantum mechanics agrees with physical measurements to within 1 part per trillion. In other words, the most successful scientific theory in the history of the world might be wrong, but chances are, it’s right. This lends some perspective to the concerns that many parents have about the science behind vaccine safety. Studies show that MMR does not cause autism, to within the margin of error afforded by studies of millions of person-years of observation. Just like proofs of quantum mechanics, there will always be some margin of error. The question comes down to balancing the incredibly small probability of error with the very real threat to health and well-being that measles represents. For more information: Gary S. Marshall, MD, is a professor of pediatrics and chief of the division of pediatric infectious diseases at Norton Children’s and the University of Louisville School of Medicine. He is the author of Healio’s Clinical Guidance module on measles and The Vaccine Handbook . He can be reached at pids@idsociety.org . news.content_zh: Healio 于 2026 年 10 月 29 日发表的文章讨论了 麻疹 在美国的死灰复燃,指出今年确诊病例已逼近 5000 例,这是 33 年来的最高水平。报告强调,目前的 暴发 是自 1991 年以来最严重的一次,当时有 55,622 例病例和 123 人死亡。这篇文章强调了 疫苗 怀疑论和错误信息在推动 传播 中的作用,特别是在未接种疫苗的学龄前儿童中。它还提到了 12 个月以下儿童感染 亚急性硬化性全脑炎 (SSPE) 的可能性,这是一种严重的神经系统并发症,估计发生率为 600 人中就有 1 人。该文章提到了一个国际委员会于 2026 年 11 月评估美国是否仍然符合 麻疹 消除标准,这一状态已保持了二十多年。该文章呼吁重新关注 麻疹 和公共卫生信息,以防止进一步传播并保护儿童免受 麻疹(包括 SSPE)的长期后果。本文还涉及了关于早期 疫苗接种 时间表的争论以及平衡 疫苗 疗效与母源抗体潜在风险的挑战。响应状态涉及持续努力解决 疫苗 犹豫并改进 监测,尽管文章指出当前的方法可能会错过学校的早期 暴发。这篇文章基于 IDWeek 上发表的专家分析和参考研究,但没有提供美国和宾夕法尼亚州以外死亡人数或病例数的具体数据。

news.content_title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
news.content: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole-genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions. “As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude. Ars Video How The Callisto Protocol's Gameplay Was Perfected Months Before Release Importations In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation. In a second importation event, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious. As a result, four residents with close contact with the South Carolina visitors fell ill. While infectious, the four residents visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church. Nine of their contacts and one person exposed in a public location fell ill, leading to a total cluster of 14 cases that spanned January 15 to February 17. In the third importation event, two state residents returned from South Carolina and fell ill on January 15 to 16. No additional cases were linked to these residents. Similarly, a fourth importation event occurred when a resident returned from travel. The person adhered to isolation and quarantine recommendations, and no cases were linked to this one. In the fifth importation event, a Washington state resident returned from out-of-state travel where they had contact with ill contacts and fell ill themselves on January 19. While contagious, they visited a school and a healthcare facility. Six close contacts fell ill. In all, this cluster of seven cases spanned January 19 to January 29. The genome sequences from five of the cases were nearly identical to those seen in South Carolina. Officials credit basic public health work of quarantines, isolation, and contact tracing with keeping the virus from spreading farther than it did. Contradicting Kennedy While the study highlights how readily this virus can spread among states amid declining vaccination, it also contradicts a common talking point from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, a prominent anti-vaccine advocate, has downplayed the current measles surge in the US and aggressively defended against suggestions that his decades of anti-vaccine misinformation and disinformation have contributed to the surge in cases and drop in vaccination. Instead, Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false . Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , only 18 of the country’s 4,588 confirmed measles cases this year were reported among international visitors. Of all the cases, 4,404 (96 percent) are linked to a domestic outbreak. The US has had 43 new outbreaks this year. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes. 58 Comments

news.content: An electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia S. Goldsmith; William Bellini, Ph.D./Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS/TNS) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: October 27, 2026 at 9:00 AM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The statewide total of confirmed measles cases has reached 1,360 across 44 counties. Berks County remains at seven cases in the update issued Monday by the sate Department of Health. The state continues to report five measles-associated deaths. A department spokesperson said the measles-associated death of a 39-year-old woman announced by the Franklin County coroner on Oct. 12 is still under investigation by department experts. The department’s update noted the following: • New positive cases since Oct. 23: 22 • Total counties: 44 • Total cumulative cases: 1,360 • Total hospitalizations: 258 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 5 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the department’s dashboard at pa.gov/measles , Lancaster County remains at the top in cases with 478. Cases in the region: Chester County, 93; Lebanon County, 21; Schuylkill County, 7; Montgomery County, 3; and Lehigh County, 2. State health center staff have administered almost 6,700 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 228 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since the outbreak began in late April, officials said. Overall, the department has given more than 10,300 MMR vaccine doses this year. Officials said healthcare providers continue to see an increase in residents interested in the MMR vaccinations. Providers typically administer about 25,000 doses of the vaccine a month. They said more than 56,000 doses were given in September and that more than 39,000 MMR vaccines were given in the first three weeks of October. Because measles continues to spread, the department said it recommends an additional early zero dose for infants between the ages of 6 and 11 months who live in or travel to counties flagged on the measles dashboard for sustained community transmission. They said the early dose does not replace the two routine doses. Children 12 months and older who have not received any dose should get one now and a second dose at least 28 days later. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a healthcare provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your healthcare provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). news.content_title: A 'canary in the coal mine': Measles resurgence exposes weaknesses in U.S. public health, experts say
news.content: Key Points More than 4,400 measles cases and at least three deaths have been reported nationwide this year, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. Several public health experts told CNBC the resurgence exposes declining vaccination rates and waning trust in health institutions as well as growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities. Those same vulnerabilities could complicate the nation’s response to future infectious disease threats, from other vaccine-preventable illnesses to emerging pathogens. watch now VIDEO 3:03 03:03 What the measles outbreak signals for the U.S. Health and Science For nearly two years, the U.S. has had to swallow an uncomfortable reality: A highly infectious disease it once eliminated is spreading again. More than 4,400 measles cases and at least three deaths have been reported nationwide this year, marking the country’s worst outbreak in more than three decades. The spike followed nearly 2,300 cases in 2025. But many public health experts argue that the return of measles isn’t the only concerning development — it’s also what the resurgence signals about America that’s causing alarm. Measles is often described as one of the most contagious viruses, and it is uniquely unforgiving of weaknesses in public health defenses. A safe and highly effective vaccine has existed for decades. But the virus’s spread exposes declining vaccination rates, eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities, experts said. Together, those vulnerabilities have made measles a revealing test of the country’s public health defenses. For some experts, the resurgence of a disease the U.S. eliminated more than two decades ago is a warning sign of its ability to contain future threats, from other vaccine-preventable diseases to emerging pathogens. “Measles is the canary in the coal mine for so many different reasons,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health. “It’s the canary in the coal mine for other vaccine-preventable illnesses, where we could see a return of things that used to harm kids, but also for very acute, no-notice dangerous infectious disease emergencies.” The U.S. is on track to lose its official measles elimination status during an upcoming review by the Pan American Health Organization , which will meet in Washington, D.C., in mid-November. “It says a lot about a country if it is unable to control measles,” said Nuzzo, who is one of 10 experts CNBC spoke with about the ongoing outbreak and its implications. Pockets of vulnerability A measles advisory is shown tacked to a bulletin board outside Gaines County Courthouse in Seminole, Texas, April 9, 2025. Brandon Bell | Getty Images The U.S. has the tools to prevent measles from spreading. But pockets of low vaccination coverage are leaving the country vulnerable. The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission. That translates to 280,000 kindergarteners who did not complete their MMR vaccination series, according to the CDC. Childhood vaccination exemptions in the U.S. also reached a record high 4.2% for incoming kindergartners during the 2025-2026 school year, up from 3.6% the previous year, the agency says. “The bottom line is that not enough people are vaccinating their kids,” said Brown’s Nuzzo. While some cases stem from international travel, much of the recent spread has been driven by local transmission in “too many” communities where vaccination coverage falls below 95%, she added. Among states across the U.S. collecting MMR vaccine data, 67% of counties and jurisdictions now have immunization rates below 95%, according to a September investigation by NBC News. Recent U.S. outbreaks have often occurred in “closely knit communities” where people have frequent contact and low vaccination coverage, said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But declining vaccination rates do not mean most Americans have turned against immunization. Polling suggests broad support for childhood vaccines. A July KFF survey found that many Americans sit in a more uncertain middle ground about the shots, leaving room for conflicting information to influence their decisions. “This is not an edge-case issue,” Nuzzo said, adding that the vast majority of parents still vaccinate their children. Even if outbreaks are concentrated in a minority of communities, it can create a “dangerous situation” far from those areas, she said. Infants too young to be vaccinated and people who cannot receive immunizations for medical reasons can be particularly vulnerable when the virus spreads into communities with high vaccination rates. Those risks come as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy. President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine be split into separate shots, while repeating false claims about its safety. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has also overhauled a key federal advisory committee responsible for recommending childhood immunizations, though the changes are frozen amid ongoing litigation. Several experts told CNBC that such moves risk further eroding confidence in vaccines and weakening efforts to protect children. Public health infrastructure was also “really decimated by Covid,” and the CDC in particular lost many experienced scientists and physicians “who had spent their lives working on vaccine-preventable diseases,” said Scott Weaver, a virologist who is the research director of Galveston National Laboratory. He added that the CDC, as of September, is also no longer immediately incorporating state-reported “measles-associated” deaths into its national published tally, making it harder to track outbreaks in real time. The agency lists three measles-related deaths in 2026, but Pennsylvania has reported at least five deaths. “We have folks in federal health leadership right now that are throwing gasoline on the fire, and that is not helping the situation,” said Jess Steier, a public health scientist and founder and CEO of Unbiased Science, an organization that aims to make complex scientific concepts understandable. Consequences beyond current outbreaks A medical assistant draws a measles, mumps and rubella vaccination to be administered to a young person at the pediatric office of Dr. Gary M. Kramer in Coral Gables, Florida, August 13, 2026. Joe Raedle | Getty Images If the U.S. fails to materially improve vaccination rates, the measles resurgence could extend beyond ongoing outbreaks. At “current” state-level vaccination rates, measles could become endemic again in the U.S., resulting in an estimated 851,300 cases over 25 years, according to a large-scale epidemiological model published in JAMA in April 2025 by researchers at Stanford and other institutions. Under that scenario, the model predicts the measles cases could lead to 170,200 hospitalizations and 2,550 deaths over that period. The model, which simulated infectious disease spread in the U.S. at various childhood vaccination levels, relies on immunization data from 2004 to 2023 for that baseline scenario. The model assumes that diseases are introduced by someone who travels abroad and brings them back, most commonly a U.S. citizen who isn’t vaccinated. While many people are currently immune through vaccination, outbreaks can increase in size and frequency if immunization rates decline over a longer period. Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist and the director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, said he views the measles situation in Canada as a direct warning for the U.S. Canada lost its official measles elimination status in November after a multi-province outbreak that generated more than 5,400 cases across 10 jurisdictions in 2025. Canada has a population of more than 40 million people. “We have a population of 350 million. If you extrapolate, if we had the very same experience that Canada had over the next year or two, that would be up to 50,000 cases of measles in the U.S.,” Osterholm said. “I think that’s a potential future we have to be mindful of.” Other vaccine-preventable diseases An even larger measles outbreak isn’t the only potential problem. Vaccination coverage for other childhood diseases has similarly declined. The share of U.S. kindergartners vaccinated against polio fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, while coverage for diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis, or DTaP, dropped to 92%, according to CDC data . The U.S. has already seen a sharp rise in pertussis, or whooping cough. U.S. reported cases reached roughly 43,300 in 2024 and nearly 28,000 in 2025, up substantially from pandemic-era levels, according to the CDC. Brown’s Nuzzo said the resurgence reflects, in part, fewer people getting vaccinated and the fact that protection from the pertussis vaccine wanes over time. The simulation model published in JAMA also examined how falling childhood immunization rates could affect the future spread of several diseases previously eliminated from the U.S. through vaccines. Under current vaccination levels, the researchers found that diseases including rubella and polio were unlikely to become endemic in the U.S. But in a hypothetical scenario in which childhood vaccination rates fell by 50%, the model projected 9.9 million cases of rubella, 4.3 million cases of polio and 197 cases of diphtheria over 25 years. Rubella can cause devastating complications when an infection during pregnancy passes to a developing fetus, while polio can cause paralysis and death, said Dr. Nathan Lo, assistant professor of infectious diseases at Stanford Medicine. The projections are not predictions that these outbreaks will occur, but they illustrate how much risks could grow if vaccination coverage deteriorates. “What vaccines often buy you is not just the protection, but also less uncertainty,” said Mathew Kiang, an assistant professor of epidemiology and population health at Stanford Medicine who also worked on the simulation model. “I think even more frightening is just the really wide uncertainty that we just wouldn’t be sure of what could happen.” Preparing for the next threat The measles resurgence is also raising questions about how effective the U.S. can be at detecting and responding to emerging public health threats before they spread. “Public health is all about prevention,” said Dr. Manisha Juthani, president of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials and commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Public Health. She said the country must maintain its ability to detect threats, invest in surveillance, and recognize that infectious diseases do not respect national borders. Those capabilities are crucial for curbing emerging pathogens, especially when scientists initially know little about how a new disease spreads, how severe it is or how to treat it. A pathogen could spread before vaccines or treatments are available, making early detection, clear public communication and coordination especially important. Other experts argue that weaknesses in those capabilities could also have implications for the country’s defenses against deliberate biological attacks. In an April 2025 op-ed , Steph Batalis, a research fellow at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, argued that the measles outbreak exposed a broader vulnerability in the U.S.′ biodefense strategy and, specifically, a weakened ability to deter potential biological attacks. She argued that the country’s struggle to contain a known, vaccine-preventable disease “might only embolden those who see our public health vulnerabilities as an opportunity.” But Osterholm, who works extensively on bioterrorism, said low MMR immunization rates and rising measles cases do not necessarily indicate that Americans would refuse a vaccine or antibiotic during a biological emergency. The shots and drugs used to counter biological threats can differ from those routinely administered to the public, he said, and the prospect of a severe outbreak could prompt urgency among the public to seek protection. That point highlights an important limitation: The measles resurgence by itself does not establish whether the U.S. could withstand entirely different or novel public health threats. But as a disease the U.S. knows how to prevent spreads, experts say the stakes of addressing those vulnerabilities extend to whatever might come next. news.title_zh: 专家称,“煤矿里的金丝雀”:麻疹 的复苏暴露了美国公共卫生的弱点 - CNBC
news.source_body_en: The U.S. is experiencing a significant measles resurgence, with over 4,400 cases and at least three deaths reported this year, marking the worst outbreak in more than three decades. Public health experts warn that this resurgence highlights declining vaccination rates, eroding trust in health institutions, and challenges in persuading people to protect themselves and their communities. The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is 97% effective after two doses, but vaccination coverage among kindergarteners dropped to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, below the recommended 95% threshold. This has left 280,000 children unvaccinated and 67% of counties with immunization rates below 95%. The resurgence is seen as a 'canary in the coal mine' for broader public health vulnerabilities, including the potential for measles to become endemic again if vaccination rates do not improve. The CDC is also facing challenges in tracking outbreaks due to its delayed reporting of measles-associated deaths. Experts argue that the current situation reflects broader issues with public health infrastructure and federal vaccine policy, which may further undermine confidence in immunizations.

news.content: A man from the Plain community harvests crops in Intercourse, Pa., on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: AP/Jessie Wardarski By The Associated Press October 30, 2026 6:02 am EPHRATA, Pa. — Lancaster County, home to the largest Amish population in the U.S., is now the epicenter of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 35 years. Vaccination rates have long been low among the Amish, and are now falling in the general population, creating the perfect conditions for the contagious virus — officially considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000 — to spread here and beyond. Pennsylvania has the most U.S. cases, with over 1,350 this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone, according to state health figures. That’s likely a big undercount, community leaders say, since many people with measles never see a doctor. The state has recorded three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties. The outbreak has especially hit the “Plain communities” of Amish and conservative Mennonites — so named for the religious groups’ modest dress and limited use of technology. Vaccination rates, and attitudes about vaccines, range widely among them. But overall, they are less likely to be vaccinated than the general population, due more to culture and habit than doctrine. The outbreak follows ones in 2025 in Mennonite populations in Texas and elsewhere. Most states have recorded cases this year. And though the Plain People avoid participating in many areas of society, they're not isolated. They interact with the general public at farmers markets, doctors' offices and elsewhere. So their new openness to vaccines after bearing the brunt of the outbreak impacts the entire community. A measles, mumps and rubella virus vaccine at Union Community Care clinic in Lancaster, Pa., on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. Credit: AP/Jessie Wardarski Here are some takeaways from The Associated Press’ reporting: While some think all Plain people reject vaccines, views actually vary Attitudes toward vaccines in Plain communities have alternately warmed and cooled over the years — most recently cooling in reaction to strict COVID-19 public health measures, according to community leaders and scholars. The measles outbreak is prompting many to accept the shots while reinforcing vaccine skepticism and suspicion in others. Those who avoid vaccines usually aren’t driven by ideology, community leaders and experts say. “There’s nothing in Amish theology or historic documents that you can find that specifically addresses or is opposed to immunization,” said Steve Nolt, director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Lancaster County. The main reason Plain people skip vaccinations isn't that they're against them, added Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite and former administrator of the Parochial Medical Center in the town of New Holland. “It was simply, ‘Well, we never did before, and we came through all right.’” Dropping vaccination rates across the US increase the threat of measles Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces. “Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.” The risk grows as vaccination rates decline — which has been happening across the nation. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20. “Though Plain communities are an easy and recognizable target, declining childhood vaccination rates in our county are not limited to the Amish,” wrote Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, in a recent commentary. “Kindergarten vaccination rates have declined in every central Pennsylvania county since 2020.” In fact, Pennsylvania’s overall kindergarten MMR vaccination rate fell to 93.2% by last year, which is below the 95% rate that makes an outbreak extremely unlikely in a community. During the COVID-19 pandemic, area doctors saw more vaccine hesitancy among patients within and outside of Plain communities. “The COVID vaccine just created a lot of distrust, a lot of conspiracy theories,” said Dr. Anne-Marie Derrico, chief medical officer at the nonprofit Union Community Care. “There’s still kind of an overall distrust of vaccines.” After a decline in trust, some minds are changing Lancaster County Commissioner Alice Yoder said public officials need to promote the message that the vaccine is safe and effective and encourage people to get it. That approach succeeded during Pennsylvania’s last measles outbreak in 1991. “There were lines of people in the Plain community that would come and get vaccinated,” she said. Dr. D. Holmes Morton, who founded the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Mifflin County — which treats Plain patients with genetic diseases — said the same is happening now. “We are having more success at having vaccine days,” he said. Ultimately, this will keep everyone safer, said Dr. Diego Hijano of St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Getting the shot is “an act of love to your community,” he said. “You will get protected yourself. But in truth, you are actually protecting everyone around you.” ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. analysis.time: The outbreak is currently ongoing, with the article published on October 30, 2026. The measles outbreak in Pennsylvania's Amish country has been reported as the nation's worst in 35 years, with the outbreak following previous ones in 2025 in Mennonite populations in Texas and elsewhere.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is centered in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, specifically in the Plain communities of Amish and conservative Mennonites. These communities are described as having a lower vaccination rate compared to the general population, and they interact with the public at farmers markets, doctors' offices, and other locations.
analysis.event: A measles outbreak has occurred in Pennsylvania's Amish country, which is now the epicenter of the nation's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. The outbreak is attributed to low vaccination rates among the Amish and Mennonites, and it has led to increased vaccine acceptance in some segments of the community.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Pennsylvania has recorded over 1,350 measles cases this year, with more than a third in Lancaster County alone. There have been three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties. The outbreak has impacted the Plain communities, which are not isolated despite their limited societal participation.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Public officials and community leaders are promoting the safety and effectiveness of the measles vaccine to encourage vaccination. Some community members are changing their views, while others remain skeptical. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) notes that declining vaccination rates increase the risk of measles outbreaks, and the outbreak is impacting the entire community.

The outbreak is linked to low vaccination rates among the Amish and conservative Mennonites, who are less likely to be vaccinated due to cultural and habitual reasons rather than religious doctrine. news.content: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Health 29 Oct 2026 8:58 pm AEDT Date Time BMJ 90% of cases occurred in historically under-vaccinated communities Findings offer insights for countries aiming to retain or regain their elimination status The outbreak that contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025 was concentrated in historically under-vaccinated communities with close social networks across Canada, the US, Mexico, and beyond, creating opportunities for cross-border transmission, concludes a study published by The BMJ today. The researchers say the findings highlight the ongoing risk of measles resurgence in countries that have previously successfully controlled the disease, and underscore the importance of culturally tailored community engagement to build trust and confidence in vaccination and prevent future outbreaks. Canada achieved measles-free status in 1998 after introducing a two-dose vaccine schedule and a national catch-up programme for school-aged children, but lost it in November 2025 after a measles outbreak that involved several provinces. In Ontario, the outbreak disproportionately affected historically under-vaccinated communities – groups with historically low vaccine coverage and close social networks across Canada, the US, and Mexico. To better understand the course of this outbreak and its impact, researchers analysed measles cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period (28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025). The outbreak consisted of 2,377 cases (2,064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks. Most cases (90%) occurred among members of historically under‐vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2,377 cases, around three quarters (73%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2,121 (89%) were unvaccinated and 97 (4%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 admissions to hospital, 13 admissions to an intensive care unit, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis (brain inflammation), and one infant death. Laboratory tests identified a distinct measles virus strain that was subsequently detected elsewhere in Canada, and in the US, Mexico, and the Netherlands due to close social ties within and between under-vaccinated communities combined with the high transmissibility of measles. The researchers acknowledge that their analysis is subject to limitations inherent to public health surveillance data, and note that the number of cases and associated complications may be higher than what is reported in the study. In addition, the proportion of cases in under-vaccinated communities is likely to be conservative, reflecting challenges in data collection for a variety of reasons, including mistrust among some community members and concerns from public health staff about the risk of stigmatization of affected groups during the outbreak. However, they say this measles outbreak illustrates the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of substantial immunity gaps within domestically and globally interconnected communities. Limited spillover beyond these communities also highlights a high degree of vaccine acceptance in the population at large and the success of local partners in closing immunity gaps as part of the outbreak response, they add. "Strengthening of immunisation systems, improving vaccine coverage, and sustaining culturally appropriate engagement to continue to build trust in immunisation will be essential to prevent future vaccine preventable disease outbreaks and to support re-establishing measles elimination," they conclude. In a linked editorial, Jennifer Nuzzo at Brown University School of Public Health warns that Canada's loss of elimination status signals growing vulnerability to infectious disease threats, even in well-resourced high-income countries. She argues that elimination requires not just high vaccination coverage, but also sensitive disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, rapid outbreak investigations, timely reporting, effective public health responses, and public trust. Failing to stop measles within national borders also makes it harder for countries around the world to keep the disease at bay, she adds. She urges countries to recommit to measles elimination "not simply to restore a designation, but to stop a dangerous, preventable disease and strengthen the public health systems that protect their own populations and those of their neighbours from other serious infectious threats." /Public Release. Most cases (90%) occurred among members of historically under‐vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2,377 cases, around three quarters (73%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2,121 (89%) were unvaccinated and 97 (4%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 admissions to hospital, 13 admissions to an intensive care unit, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis (brain inflammation), and one infant death. Laboratory tests identified a distinct measles virus strain that was subsequently detected elsewhere in Canada, and in the US, Mexico, and the Netherlands due to close social ties within and between under-vaccinated communities combined with the high transmissibility of measles. The researchers acknowledge that their analysis is subject to limitations inherent to public health surveillance data, and note that the number of cases and associated complications may be higher than what is reported in the study. In addition, the proportion of cases in under-vaccinated communities is likely to be conservative, reflecting challenges in data collection for a variety of reasons, including mistrust among some community members and concerns from public health staff about the risk of stigmatization of affected groups during the outbreak. However, they say this measles outbreak illustrates the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of substantial immunity gaps within domestically and globally interconnected communities. Limited spillover beyond these communities also highlights a high degree of vaccine acceptance in the population at large and the success of local partners in closing immunity gaps as part of the outbreak response, they add. "Strengthening of immunisation systems, improving vaccine coverage, and sustaining culturally appropriate engagement to continue to build trust in immunisation will be essential to prevent future vaccine preventable disease outbreaks and to support re-establishing measles elimination," they conclude. In a linked editorial, Jennifer Nuzzo at Brown University School of Public Health warns that Canada's loss of elimination status signals growing vulnerability to infectious disease threats, even in well-resourced high-income countries. She argues that elimination requires not just high vaccination coverage, but also sensitive disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, rapid outbreak investigations, timely reporting, effective public health responses, and public trust. Failing to stop measles within national borders also makes it harder for countries around the world to keep the disease at bay, she adds. She urges countries to recommit to measles elimination "not simply to restore a designation, but to stop a dangerous, preventable disease and strengthen the public health systems that protect their own populations and those of their neighbours from other serious infectious threats." /Public Release. Read Full Bio Dan Raby October 27, 2026 / 4:23 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Georgia health officials have confirmed three new cases of measles connected to a previous case earlier in October. The Georgia Department of Public Health said the three new cases confirmed in Macon County were close contacts of a previous case in the county confirmed on Oct. 12. The three new infected individuals were all unvaccinated. Investigators say they are working to notify others who may have been exposed to the virus. While details about the original case remain limited, officials say he or she had contact with a confirmed measles case in Pennsylvania, where the state reports an ongoing outbreak of the virus with more than 1,100 cases. Authorities believe the individual visited a LongHorn Steakhouse on Hampton Court in Perry on the night of Oct. 7 while they were infectious. The agency is urging anyone who was there during that window to check their vaccination status and watch for symptoms through Oct. 28. The new cases bring Georgia's total measles count this year to 25. Last year, the state reported 10 cases. Measles aka morbilli and rubeola is a highly contagious viral disease. It starts with a high fever, cough, and red eyes InnerVerse / Getty Images Possible signs of measles exposure and what you should do Measles first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes, and a rash. The rash generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and then spreading downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. When the rash appears, the fever may spike over 104 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The virus is highly contagious, spreads through the air, and can stay on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has been in a room. If you become sick or believe you have been exposed to measles, contact your healthcare provider immediately but do not go to the doctor's office without first letting them know about your symptoms. You can also call the Georgia Department of Public Health's Acute Disease Epidemiology Section at 404-657-2588 during business hours, Monday through Friday, or 1-866-782-4584 after hours on evenings and weekends. news.content_title: Canada's measles outbreak exposes vulnerabilities in disease elimination efforts
news.content: The outbreak that contributed to Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025 was concentrated in historically under-vaccinated communities with close social networks across Canada, the US, Mexico, and beyond, creating opportunities for cross-border transmission, concludes a study published by The BMJ today. The researchers say the findings highlight the ongoing risk of measles resurgence in countries that have previously successfully controlled the disease, and underscore the importance of culturally tailored community engagement to build trust and confidence in vaccination and prevent future outbreaks. Canada achieved measles-free status in 1998 after introducing a two-dose vaccine schedule and a national catch-up programme for school-aged children, but lost it in November 2025 after a measles outbreak that involved several provinces. In Ontario, the outbreak disproportionately affected historically under-vaccinated communities - groups with historically low vaccine coverage and close social networks across Canada, the US, and Mexico. To better understand the course of this outbreak and its impact, researchers analysed measles cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period (28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025). The outbreak consisted of 2,377 cases (2,064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks. Most cases (90%) occurred among members of historically under‐vaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. Among the 2,377 cases, around three quarters (73%) occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger, 2,121 (89%) were unvaccinated and 97 (4%) had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 admissions to hospital, 13 admissions to an intensive care unit, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis (brain inflammation ), and one infant death. Laboratory tests identified a distinct measles virus strain that was subsequently detected elsewhere in Canada, and in the US, Mexico, and the Netherlands due to close social ties within and between under-vaccinated communities combined with the high transmissibility of measles. The researchers acknowledge that their analysis is subject to limitations inherent to public health surveillance data, and note that the number of cases and associated complications may be higher than what is reported in the study. In addition, the proportion of cases in under-vaccinated communities is likely to be conservative, reflecting challenges in data collection for a variety of reasons, including mistrust among some community members and concerns from public health staff about the risk of stigmatization of affected groups during the outbreak. However, they say this measles outbreak illustrates the fragility of measles elimination in the presence of substantial immunity gaps within domestically and globally interconnected communities. Limited spillover beyond these communities also highlights a high degree of vaccine acceptance in the population at large and the success of local partners in closing immunity gaps as part of the outbreak response, they add. "Strengthening of immunisation systems, improving vaccine coverage, and sustaining culturally appropriate engagement to continue to build trust in immunisation will be essential to prevent future vaccine preventable disease outbreaks and to support re-establishing measles elimination," they conclude. In a linked editorial, Jennifer Nuzzo at Brown University School of Public Health warns that Canada's loss of elimination status signals growing vulnerability to infectious disease threats, even in well-resourced high-income countries. She argues that elimination requires not just high vaccination coverage, but also sensitive disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, rapid outbreak investigations, timely reporting, effective public health responses, and public trust. Failing to stop measles within national borders also makes it harder for countries around the world to keep the disease at bay, she adds. She urges countries to recommit to measles elimination "not simply to restore a designation, but to stop a dangerous, preventable disease and strengthen the public health systems that protect their own populations and those of their neighbours from other serious infectious threats." Source: Journal reference: Wilson, S. E., et al . (2026). Impact of a large measles outbreak associated with transmission in the Americas and Canada’s loss of measles elimination status: Descriptive cohort study. BMJ. DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2026-101123. https://www.bmj.com/lookup/doi/10.1136/bmj-2026-101123

analysis.time: The outbreak was reported from 28 October 2024 to 6 October 2025, with Canada losing its measles elimination status in November 2025. The publication date of the news report is 2026-10-28.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak was concentrated in historically under-vaccinated communities across Canada, the US, Mexico, and beyond, with a disproportionate impact in Ontario. The affected population included individuals aged 19 years or younger, with 2,121 unvaccinated cases and 97 with unknown vaccination status.
analysis.event: A measles outbreak occurred in Canada, leading to the loss of its measles elimination status. The outbreak involved several provinces and was associated with cross-border transmission due to close social networks. The event was confirmed by a study published in The BMJ.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The outbreak resulted in 2,377 cases (2,064 confirmed and 313 probable), 166 hospital admissions, 13 ICU admissions, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis, and one infant death. The risk of measles resurgence was highlighted due to immunity gaps and cross-border transmission.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The researchers analyzed cases reported to Ontario's public health surveillance system during the outbreak period. They acknowledged limitations in data collection, including mistrust among community members and concerns about stigmatization. The outbreak response included efforts to close immunity gaps and improve public health systems.

analysis.brief_en: A measles outbreak in Canada, which led to the country losing its measles elimination status in November 2025, has exposed vulnerabilities in disease control efforts. The outbreak was concentrated in historically under-vaccinated communities across Canada, the US, and Mexico, with limited spillover into the broader population. Over 2,377 cases were reported, including 2,121 unvaccinated individuals and 97 with unknown vaccination status. The outbreak resulted in 166 hospital admissions, 13 ICU admissions, 51 infections during pregnancy, 10 congenital measles infections, one case of encephalitis, and one infant death. Researchers analyzed data from Ontario's public health surveillance system, noting limitations in data collection due to mistrust and concerns about stigmatization. The study highlights the importance of culturally tailored community engagement and robust surveillance to prevent future outbreaks. The outbreak underscores the fragility of measles elimination in interconnected communities and the need for sustained public health efforts.

analysis.brief_en: On October 30, 2026, Contagion Live reported an increase in measles PCR testing, noting that positivity rates have risen in national lab data. The article highlights the ongoing monitoring of measles cases through laboratory testing, but it does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. The situation is described as under investigation, with no further details on the scale or risk level of the outbreak. The focus is on the testing methods and the observed trend in positivity rates, indicating a need for continued surveillance and analysis. This update is part of a broader discussion on measles and its clinical implications, including treatment and hospitalization considerations. The article does not mention any hard exclusions or related entities, and the evidence is based on the measles virus as the primary target.

news.source_body_en: On October 30, 2026, Contagion Live reported an increase in measles PCR testing, noting that positivity rates have risen in national lab data. The article highlights the ongoing monitoring of measles cases through laboratory testing, but it does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers. The situation is described as under investigation, with no further details on the scale or risk level of the outbreak. The focus is on the testing methods and the observed trend in positivity rates, indicating a need for continued surveillance and analysis. This update is part of a broader discussion on measles and its clinical implications, including treatment and hospitalization considerations. The article does not mention any hard exclusions or related entities, and the evidence is based on the measles virus as the primary target.

supplementary_news.content_title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
supplementary_news.content: Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions. In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread. South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it. The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole-genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions. “As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude. Ars Video Importations In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation. In a second importation event, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious. As a result, four residents with close contact with the South Carolina visitors fell ill. While infectious, the four residents visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church. Nine of their contacts and one person exposed in a public location fell ill, leading to a total cluster of 14 cases that spanned January 15 to February 17. In the third importation event, two state residents returned from South Carolina and fell ill on January 15 to 16. No additional cases were linked to these residents. Similarly, a fourth importation event occurred when a resident returned from travel. The person adhered to isolation and quarantine recommendations, and no cases were linked to this one. In the fifth importation event, a Washington state resident returned from out-of-state travel where they had contact with ill contacts and fell ill themselves on January 19. While contagious, they visited a school and a healthcare facility. Six close contacts fell ill. In all, this cluster of seven cases spanned January 19 to January 29. The genome sequences from five of the cases were nearly identical to those seen in South Carolina. Officials credit basic public health work of quarantines, isolation, and contact tracing with keeping the virus from spreading farther than it did. Contradicting Kennedy While the study highlights how readily this virus can spread among states amid declining vaccination, it also contradicts a common talking point from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, a prominent anti-vaccine advocate, has downplayed the current measles surge in the US and aggressively defended against suggestions that his decades of anti-vaccine misinformation and disinformation have contributed to the surge in cases and drop in vaccination. Instead, Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false . Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , only 18 of the country’s 4,588 confirmed measles cases this year were reported among international visitors. Of all the cases, 4,404 (96 percent) are linked to a domestic outbreak. The US has had 43 new outbreaks this year. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. She specializes in covering infectious diseases, public health, and microbes. 58 Comments
